recipes.title: Comparing a dollar figure across STATES, not just across years
recipes.body:
adjust_inflation deflates against ONE national CPI series — it removes economy-wide inflation over TIME, but every state is still assumed to face the same prices. That is correct for comparing one place across years; it is NOT a cost-of-living adjustment, because it does not account for a dollar buying more in Mississippi than in California in the same year.

A genuine state-to-state real-income or real-growth comparison needs a SECOND, independent step: divide by each state's own value in econ.regional_price_parities (BEA RPP, all-items, US=100 baseline) for that year. The two adjustments answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other:

  1. adjust_inflation(nominal, year) -> real national dollars (removes time-inflation only)
  2. real_national_dollars / (regional_price_parities.value / 100) -> real, cost-of-living-adjusted dollars (removes the cross-state price-level gap too)

Skip step 2 and a result that says 'adjusted for cost of living' has actually only done step 1 - a national-inflation adjustment wearing a cost-of-living label. This is not a hypothetical: measured directly in this harness, an analysis that applied RPP alone (skipping adjust_inflation) reported a state's growth lead as 'surviving the cost-of-living check' when two independent analyses that applied BOTH steps found the same lead did NOT survive - same RPP table, different arithmetic, opposite conclusion.

Do both steps, in that order, whenever the question compares places, not just times. Name which state(s) the ranking is sensitive to if the two adjustments move the answer versus a national-inflation-only adjustment - that sensitivity is itself part of the answer, not a footnote.

recipes.title: Grouping states/entities by a category with more than one reasonable definition, or that can CHANGE during the analysis window
recipes.body:
Two separate, compounding traps live here, and a caller usually only guards against one of them.

TRAP 1 - the definition itself is ambiguous. 'Represented by Republicans' could mean presidential vote, governor's party, legislative trifecta, or congressional delegation, and these disagree on real states (Michigan/Pennsylvania/Wisconsin/Arizona/Nevada/Georgia split their governor and 2024-presidential labels). Picking one without checking whether the conclusion survives a different reasonable definition is a hidden researcher-degree-of-freedom - it makes the choice of definition invisible, when it was actually doing some of the analytical work. FIX: run the comparison under at least two independent definitions and report whether the result agrees. In this harness, cross-checking 'current governor party' against '2024 presidential winner' surfaced the same modest, non-significant gap under both - real corroboration, not just one number dressed up as settled.

TRAP 2 - a classification is not fixed for the length of a multi-year window; some states flip during it. CHECK FIRST whether officials.state_political_index (SPI) already carries a year dimension in the loaded schema (describe_table it - the table has been extended to compute the score per year rather than only a single current-Congress snapshot). If it has a year column, query it for each year in your window directly - that is the correct fix, not a workaround. Only fall back to hand-building a multi-snapshot classification (take snapshots at the window's start AND end from a source that is NOT already time-varying, e.g. electoral_college_votes; classify a unit into a stable category only if it held that category at every snapshot; give every unit that changed its OWN separate 'Swing'/'Transitional' bucket rather than forcing it into either stable group, and report that bucket's own result - it is not noise to discard) if describe_table shows SPI is still single-snapshot in the version you are running against. Measured directly in this harness, before a by-year SPI was available: classifying states by whether the same party won their electoral votes at both a window's opening and closing elections showed the 'Swing' bucket grew fastest of the three groups - a finding a single-snapshot classification hides entirely, and exactly the kind of result a by-year SPI query should now surface without the manual workaround.

Both traps generalize past partisan control to any question grouping states/entities by a status that can be defined more than one way or can change mid-window: regulatory regime, union representation, right-to-work status, sanctuary-city designation, and similar. Whichever way you classify, correlating the outcome against SPI's continuous -100..+100 score directly is a good check alongside a categorical split - a weak or null correlation there confirms a categorical near-tie isn't an artifact of where a group boundary was drawn.

recipes.title: Averaging or trending crime.cde_offenses across a multi-year window
recipes.body:
crime.cde_offenses carries population_coverage_pct (percentage of the state's population covered by agencies that actually reported that month) precisely because the underlying FBI collection is not one consistent series across a long window. The FBI phased agencies off the legacy Summary Reporting System (SRS) onto NIBRS-only reporting between roughly 2018 and 2021, and a number of large agencies - including some in populous states - had periods of non-reporting during the transition. Averaging or summing offense_rate across years that straddle this transition without checking coverage risks treating a reporting-coverage artifact as a real crime-rate change: a state's apparent multi-year rate can shift because fewer agencies reported, not because violence changed.

Before trusting a multi-year average or trend built from cde_offenses: query population_coverage_pct per state per year in the window and flag any year where it drops materially relative to its neighbors for that state - that year's rate is not on the same footing as the others and either needs a caveat or should be reported separately rather than blended into one average. This is a warehouse-native check (no external research needed): the column already carries exactly the signal that makes the SRS-to-NIBRS transition visible.

Measured directly in this harness: an unaided persona researching this same transition from published literature flagged it as a real caveat on a 2018-2024 multi-year crime-rate average; the askamerica-connector run answering the same question in the same session used a 2019-2025 sum across cde_offenses without checking population_coverage_pct at all - the connector had the exact field needed to verify this and did not use it. Generalizes beyond crime: any agency-reported (not survey-sampled) series that depends on many independent reporters is vulnerable to the same coverage-drift trap whenever its collection method or covered-agency set changed within the window - check for a coverage/reporting-completeness column before averaging across a long span, not just a coverage-window column.

AND WHEN YOU DO EXCLUDE: report what the exclusion changed, not only that you made it. Compute the aggregate both ways - with and without the low-coverage periods - and state the delta. Measured here: Alaska's ten-year mean violent-crime rate is 783 per 100k over all ten years and 805 once low-coverage state-years are dropped, a 22-point swing on one state, and the direction is systematic because the filter only ever removes under-reported periods. See report-what-an-exclusion-changed-not-only-that-you-made-one for the general rule.

recipes.title: Voter turnout: use VEP (voting-eligible population), not CPS self-report or citizen-voting-age population
recipes.body:
Three different populations get called "turnout" and they give materially different numbers for the same state/year: (1) Census CPS Voting and Registration Supplement's SELF-REPORTED turnout among the citizen voting-age population - known to systematically OVER-report relative to actual counted votes (social-desirability bias in the survey); (2) citizen voting-age population (CVAP) itself as a denominator, which is not the same universe as VEP; (3) voting-eligible population (VEP, the McDonald/US Elections Project standard) = voting-age population adjusted to EXCLUDE ineligible felons and non-citizens and INCLUDE eligible overseas citizens - this is the standard denominator political scientists and the literature (Cantoni & Pons; Grimmer & Yoder) actually use.

Measured directly in this harness: a question asking for the turnout gap between strict-photo-ID and non-ID states was answered using census.cps_voting_supplement (self-reported CVAP turnout) as the denominator, producing a 2.5-point gap. Two independently-run unaided arms on the same question instead paired real vote totals (officials.presidential_election_results, FEC-sourced) with a VEP-style population denominator (University of Florida Election Lab / McDonald's dataset) and found a materially smaller 0.6-2.0 point gap, not statistically significant. The connector's own search_catalog call for 'election' had already surfaced officials.presidential_election_results in the same session - the correct raw ingredient was sitting in the search results and was never followed up on because a plausible-looking CPS table was opened first and never questioned.

FIX: for any voter-turnout question, do not default to the first table with 'voting' or 'turnout' in its name or description. Check whether the table's denominator is genuinely VEP - if it is a CPS self-report series or a raw voting-age/citizen-voting-age count, that is the wrong substitution even though it looks like a natural fit and the numbers look plausible. Prefer pairing real vote totals (e.g. officials.presidential_election_results or equivalent FEC/certified-results tables) with a VEP-style population figure over relying on a self-reported survey turnout rate.

recipes.title: Multiple candidate predictors that could explain the same outcome - check they aren't just proxies for each other
recipes.body:
When a question offers several plausible drivers of the same outcome (density, urban_share, and region for a policy outcome; coal share and gas share for an electricity-price outcome), the plausible-but-wrong shortcut is to run each one through ols_regression or corr() separately and report whichever comes back with the strongest coefficient or correlation - treating each candidate as independent evidence. They usually are not independent: urban areas ARE dense, coal-heavy grids ARE often the same grids with cheap gas, so a predictor's coefficient can be large purely because it is standing in for a correlated partner, not because it has its own effect.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question with three candidate lenses (density, urban_share, region), the strongest-scoring run never checked whether the three were substitutes for each other before reporting the winning lens as the explanation. A separate question building a combined 'coal+gas' predictor never decomposed it into its components (coal r=0.85, gas r=-0.20 against the outcome in that run) - the combined variable's coefficient was reported as if it reflected one mechanism, when it was averaging two opposite-signed ones.

FIX: before treating multiple candidate predictors as separate evidence, or before building a combined variable out of several raw ones, run correlation_matrix over all the candidates together. A high pairwise correlation is a partial warning; a high VIF (>10, or >5 worth flagging) is the real one - it means a predictor's variance is almost entirely explained by the OTHERS in the set, not just by any one of them, which corr() checked pairwise won't show. Report the VIF alongside any regression that used these predictors, and decompose a combined variable into its parts with correlation_matrix or ols_regression before ascribing an effect to the combination.

BUT DO NOT LET THIS SWALLOW THE ZERO-ORDER TABLE. The warning above is about not treating separate bivariate correlations as INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE, and about not crowning whichever scores highest. It is not a reason to skip reporting them. A multivariate coefficient answers 'does this predictor matter net of the others'; a zero-order correlation answers 'which of these candidates is most associated with the outcome at all', and those two questions can rank the candidates differently. A reader asking 'what kind of place has more X' is usually asking the second one, and a question that asks in so many words for coefficients 'with N, ranked by |r|' is asking for it explicitly.

Measured directly in this harness, three questions running (2026-09-02, q4/q5/q6): the winning run went straight to a multivariate model each time and never produced the ranked pairwise table its question asked for, while two unaided arms with no connector produced bivariate r values unprompted on the same questions. The model was the better analysis; the table was the thing asked for. They are complements, and skipping the simpler one is not rigour.

FIX, additive to the above: run correlation_matrix over the candidate set (you are calling it for the VIF check anyway) and report each candidate's zero-order correlation with the outcome, with N, ordered by |r| — THEN present the multivariate model and say where the two disagree. Where a predictor's rank falls between the two, that gap is itself the finding: it is the direct measurement of how much of that candidate's apparent association was being carried by a correlated partner. State it rather than letting the model silently overwrite the raw ranking.

recipes.title: A relationship can be real and monotonic without being linear - test the shape, not just the slope
triggers: does more X mean more Q
recipes.body:
corr() and ols_regression's coefficient both summarize a relationship as a single straight line. That line can look weak or ambiguous (a middling r, a marginally significant coefficient) even when the underlying relationship is genuinely there but not linear - a threshold below which nothing happens, a plateau at the high end, or a pattern that only shows up when the predictor is grouped into ranges. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is to conclude 'no clear relationship' from a middling linear correlation without checking whether the outcome actually moves consistently as the predictor increases.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question relating a continuous predictor to an outcome, the run that won reported both a reverse-causality check (swapping which variable was treated as outcome vs. predictor) and a quintile-binned dose-response test showing the outcome trending consistently across bins - richer evidence than a single linear correlation, and evidence a plain corr() call cannot produce.

FIX: when a linear correlation comes back weak, ambiguous, or when the question specifically asks whether more of something consistently means more of the outcome (a dose-response framing), run quantile_binning_test instead of stopping at corr(). It bins the predictor into quantile groups (quintiles by default) and reports each bin's mean outcome plus whether the trend across bins is monotonic and statistically significant - this can be a real, reportable finding even when the observation-level linear r looks unimpressive, and its absence (a non-monotonic, bin-to-bin-inconsistent pattern) is itself worth reporting rather than assumed away.

recipes.title: An aggregate finding may be one subgroup wearing a group-level label - quantify the share before generalizing
triggers: which state accounts for most of
recipes.body:
A total broken out by subgroup (an agency-level rule count, a sector-level emissions total, a state-level spending figure) is often reported and discussed as if it reflects the group broadly - 'DOT issued more rules than any other department' - when in practice one subgroup can be carrying nearly the whole total. Eyeballing a GROUP BY ... ORDER BY result for the largest row answers 'which subgroup is biggest' but not 'how much of the total is this subgroup alone', which is the number that actually supports or undercuts a claim about the group as a whole.

Measured directly in this harness: a question about a department-level rule count needed the specific finding that one sub-agency (FAA) accounted for 91% of its parent department's total - a number that required a manual SUM, a per-group SUM, and a subtraction to produce, and the run that won had to hand-compute it because no tool did it directly.

FIX: whenever a group-level total is being generalized to the group ('this department is unusually active', 'this sector drives the trend'), run subgroup_contribution on the underlying value/group columns before making the claim. It reports each subgroup's share of the total AND what the total would be with that subgroup excluded in one call - if one subgroup's share is large, the finding belongs to that subgroup specifically, not to the group-level label it's filed under.

recipes.title: A conclusion built on one fixed assumption (a price, a rate, a benchmark constant) needs to be checked across the plausible range
triggers: does the conclusion hold across assumptions
recipes.body:
A comparison that depends on an assumed constant - a gasoline price used to compute a comparison's cost side, a discount rate used to compound a multi-year figure, a conversion factor - is often computed at exactly one value of that constant and reported as if the conclusion were unconditional. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is picking one reasonable-looking value (a current spot price, a round discount rate) and treating whatever comes out as THE answer, without checking whether a different but equally defensible value would change it.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question comparing electric-vehicle to gasoline-vehicle costs, the run that won tested multiple plausible gasoline-price benchmarks and found the EV lost the comparison in 9 states at one benchmark that a single-benchmark analysis never surfaced - the run that used only one gasoline price missed this entirely, not because its arithmetic was wrong, but because it never tested whether the conclusion was assumption-dependent.

FIX: when a computed conclusion rests on one fixed assumption a caller chose (rather than a value read directly from data), run scenario_sweep across a plausible range of that assumption instead of computing it once. It reruns the same query once per swept value and reports the aggregate's min, max, and whether it ever changes sign across the range - report the range alongside the point estimate, and flag explicitly if the conclusion (not just the magnitude) is sensitive to the assumption.

recipes.title: A regression coefficient that stays 'significant' after adding one control may still be explained away by controlling harder
recipes.body:
Adding one control variable to ols_regression and checking whether the coefficient of interest is still statistically significant is a real check, but a coefficient that survives ONE added control can still be substantially explained by it - 'still significant' and 'collapses to near zero' are both possible outcomes of controlling, and a p<0.05 residual coefficient can hide a relationship that is mostly, not entirely, explained by the control.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question testing whether a bivariate relationship held up under a control, the run that used ols_regression with the control added left a residual significant coefficient and reported the relationship as holding; a more thorough run instead showed the relationship collapsing to a near-zero, non-significant partial correlation once the same control was properly netted out - same control variable, different depth of adjustment, opposite headline conclusion.

FIX: when the question is specifically 'does this relationship survive controlling for Z' rather than 'what is the effect size of X on Y holding Z fixed', run partial_correlation instead of reading the coefficient off an ols_regression call. It reports the correlation between x and y AFTER regressing each on the controls, alongside the plain zero-order correlation for comparison - the gap between the two numbers, not just whether the partial one crosses p=0.05, is the finding a caller should report.

recipes.title: A question that names one likely cause still needs the leading alternative explanation tested, not assumed away
triggers: is it really X causing this
recipes.body:
A question that names or implies a likely cause ('is migration driving this county's growth') is easy to answer by confirming that cause is present and stopping - the number moved, the named factor was also moving, so the named factor gets the credit. That skips the check that actually establishes causation over correlation: is the COMPETING explanation weaker, or was it never tested at all? A trend can have more than one plausible driver (domestic migration vs. international migration; supply vs. demand; a policy change vs. a pre-existing trend), and reporting the one the question happened to name without comparing it against the alternative is confirmation, not analysis.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question about what was driving a county's population growth, the run that used a two-point stock comparison (population level at two ACS vintages) reported migration generally as the driver and never decomposed it further. A more thorough run built a full annual panel AND directly tested domestic migration against international migration as competing drivers, finding domestic migration far more strongly correlated with the growth (r=0.95) than international migration (r=0.13) - a materially more specific and better-supported finding that the two-point comparison never had the resolution to produce.

FIX: when a question implies or names a likely cause, identify the leading alternative explanation before concluding - use correlation_matrix or ols_regression to compare the named factor against its alternative(s) directly, on a full time panel rather than a two-point before/after snapshot wherever the data supports one. Report which explanation is better supported AND by how much, not just that the named one is 'also present'.

recipes.title: A state/county patent-activity table can be inventor-based or assignee-based - verify which, don't infer it from an outlier state
recipes.body:
Patent-count tables by geography are built on one of two different bases that answer different questions: INVENTOR-based (credits the patent to where the actual inventor(s) live/work - a genuine measure of where innovation happens) or ASSIGNEE-based (credits the patent to the company that owns the IP, i.e. corporate HQ or a subsidiary's registered address - a measure of corporate ownership, not innovation activity). The two produce very different geographic pictures: Delaware, Nevada, and DC are classic assignee-basis distortions, since many companies incorporate or register IP-holding subsidiaries there regardless of where any inventing happened.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question built specifically around this distinction, one run inferred that patents.patent_activity_by_county was assignee-based FROM Delaware's outlier behavior in the query results, rather than checking the table's actual documented construction - treating an observed pattern as proof of a mechanism instead of verifying the mechanism directly. A more thorough run instead sourced a table explicitly documented as inventor-residence-based (USPTO PTMT via FRED) and got a materially different geographic answer.

FIX: before answering any state/county patent-activity question, call describe_table (or read the table's catalog description) to determine whether the table is inventor-based or assignee-based - do not infer this from which states look like outliers in the results, since an outlier is consistent with either basis for different reasons. If Delaware, Nevada, or DC rank unusually high, treat that as a prompt to verify the table's basis explicitly, not as confirmation of one.

recipes.title: The question asks for a ranked exposure/risk/vulnerability score built from two or more separately computed components - combine them, don't just report each one
recipes.body:
A question asking which unit (state, county, sector) is 'most exposed' or 'most at risk' along two or more named dimensions (e.g. volume of activity AND severity of disruption) is asking for ONE combined ranking, not two separate tables. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is computing each component well - a real volume figure from one table, a real severity figure from another - and reporting both side by side, leaving the reader to eyeball which units rank high on both. That answers 'what are the components' but not the question actually asked, which is the RANK.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking which states face the biggest grain-export exposure to a shipping chokepoint, one run computed a genuine primary volume figure (state export tonnage and water-dependent share, from Commodity Flow Survey microdata) - a real, novel data point - but never combined it with a severity measure into the ranked exposure score the visual guidance asked for. A different run explicitly built a two-component composite (a volume score plus a 0-10 severity score) and ranked units on the combined figure, and was judged the more complete answer specifically because it produced the requested STRUCTURE, not just correct component data.

FIX: once each component is computed per unit, normalize each onto a common 0-1 scale before combining - raw units rarely share a scale (bushels vs. a 0-10 severity rating) and combining un-normalized values lets whichever component has the larger raw range dominate the score regardless of its actual importance. Use MIN-MAX scaling per column ((value - min) / (max - min)) via plain SQL window functions, combine with an equal weighting unless the question implies otherwise, and rank on the combined score - report each component's normalized value alongside the combined rank so a reader can see which dimension is driving which unit's position.

recipes.title: A national condition-migration trend (Good/Fair/Poor, or similar) that decelerates but doesn't reverse needs a state/entity breakdown and a quantified funding-lag figure, not just the national aggregate
recipes.body:
A national multi-point condition-migration series (share of units moving from Poor to Fair to Good over several snapshots) that shows deceleration rather than reversal is easy to report at the national level and stop - 'the improvement continued but slowed'. That is correct but thin: the question is usually really asking WHY it slowed, and the national aggregate alone answers only THAT it slowed.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question about why a national infrastructure-condition improvement decelerated, one run independently reproduced the same multi-point national series another run used (strong corroboration on the numbers) but reported a thinner treatment - it named the Good/Fair/Poor migration pattern and a brief funding note, without breaking the migration out by state to find which states were diverging from the national pattern, and without quantifying the specific funding-obligation gap. The more complete run added the state-level divergence AND a specific obligated-vs-spent dollar figure for the relevant funding program (a precise fraction of the total appropriation actually obligated to date) - the deceleration story became 'X states are stalling because Y, and only Z of the total funding has actually been obligated' rather than 'the national rate slowed'.

FIX: once a national condition-migration deceleration is established from a multi-point series, do two more things before calling the analysis complete: (1) break the same migration out by state/entity and name which units diverge from the national pattern (accelerating or stalling against it), and (2) if funding availability is part of the causal story, quantify the specific obligated-vs-authorized or spent-vs-appropriated gap for the funding program in question as a real number, not a qualitative 'funding takes time to reach construction' statement.

recipes.title: A question naming a category by year/event ('the banks that failed in 2023', 'the hurricanes that hit Florida last year') can silently mean a smaller famous subset instead of the true full population - check the count before answering
triggers: how did the X that Y differ
compared to the ones that survived
recipes.body:
A question about 'the Xs that Y'd in [time period]' - banks that failed in a given year, companies that went bankrupt, storms that made landfall, products that were recalled - is easy to answer with only the well-known, headline-generating cases, because those are what search results and public memory surface first. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is treating the famous subset as if it were the whole population without checking, especially when the famous cases share an obvious common story (a bank run, a supply-chain failure) that makes for a clean, complete-feeling answer on its own.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking how 2023's failed banks differed from survivors beforehand, three of four independently-run arms answered exclusively for the three famous large failures (SVB, Signature Bank, First Republic) without checking whether that was the complete list. Only one run verified the actual population against the FDIC's own Failed Bank List and found FIVE 2023 failures, not three - two additional small banks (one felled by alleged CEO fraud, one by concentrated single-industry loan losses) with causes entirely unrelated to the uninsured-deposit/duration-mismatch story that explained the famous three. A question phrased generically ('the banks that failed') that gets answered only for the famous subset is answering a different, narrower, easier question than the one asked - the same failure mode as this harness's answers_the_question rubric dimension names directly.

FIX: before answering a 'the Xs that Y'd in [period]' question, verify the actual count against an authoritative source (the primary regulator's own published list via describe_table/search_catalog if it exists in the corpus, or the regulator's own web list rather than a search-summary count) - do not assume a web-search or memory-recalled count is complete, and do not assume the famous cases ARE the full list just because they dominate coverage. If the full population differs materially from the well-known cases, say so explicitly and give the less-famous entries their own accounting rather than silently dropping them - which outliers exist, and why they don't fit the main story, can itself be part of the answer.

recipes.title: A question asking 'how much of [a spread/gap/change] happened in period A vs. period B' needs a direct decomposition of that spread - not a substitution of a more popular narrative framing (political, demographic) for it
triggers: which period drove more of the
did the gap widen or narrow
recipes.body:
A question that literally asks 'how much of [a measured spread/gap/change] is attributable to period A vs. period B' has a direct, computable answer - a variance decomposition, or a before/after comparison of a dispersion statistic like the coefficient of variation - that doesn't require picking a cause first. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is reaching immediately for whatever narrative framing the published literature on the topic already emphasizes (e.g. a political red-state/blue-state story) and answering THAT instead, because the framing is compelling and well-sourced - without ever computing the literal decomposition the question asked for.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking how much of the state-to-state spread in COVID death rates came before vaccines vs. after, three of four independently-run arms (including the connector-equipped one) spent most of their analytical effort on a red-state/blue-state comparison - a real, well-supported secondary finding, but an answer to a different question ('did political lean predict who got worse'), not the one literally asked. Only one run computed a direct variance decomposition of each state's cumulative rate into pre-vaccine-era variance, post-vaccine-era variance, and a covariance term from states swapping rank between eras (~55%/22%/22% in that case, with a near-zero pre/post rank correlation showing almost no state was bad in both eras) - a clean, literal answer to 'how much of the spread' that required no political classification at all. The connector-equipped run DID compute a legitimate partial answer (a before/after comparison of the coefficient of variation) but still treated the political angle as the main analysis rather than leading with the direct decomposition.

FIX: when a question asks how much of a measured spread/gap/change happened in one period vs. another, compute a direct decomposition first - a variance decomposition across periods, or a CV/range comparison before vs. after the dividing point - and report that as the primary answer. A popular narrative framing the literature already emphasizes (political, demographic, geographic) is a legitimate and often valuable SECOND layer, but present it as a separate, clearly-labeled analysis, not a substitute for the literal decomposition asked for.

recipes.title: A question asking for a specific empirical lead/lag time between two series needs a fitted correlation or a direct computation - not a summed physical-pipeline estimate (transit time + processing time + ...)
triggers: how long does it take for
recipes.body:
A question asking 'by how long does X lead Y' (port import volumes leading retail inventory, rig counts leading production, a leading economic indicator leading its target) is easy to answer by summing the physical stages of the pipeline between the two events - transit time, processing time, handoff delays - and reporting the total as the 'lead time'. That is a plausible engineering estimate, but it is not the same thing as the MEASURED lag between the two actual data series, and the two can diverge substantially, because the summed-stages estimate misses real-world friction (order-placement lead time before the physical pipeline even starts, inventory buffer policy, replenishment cadence) that only shows up in the measured relationship.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking how long port import volumes lead retail inventory build-ups, two of three unaided/partially-aided arms (plus the connector-equipped one) reached for a summed-stages estimate (ocean transit + customs + inland trucking, totaling 4-10 weeks) and never found the directly-on-point peer-reviewed study - one of those arms explicitly searched for a fitted lag study and reported, wrongly, that none exists. The two arms that DID find it (one via literature search, one by independently computing its own cross-correlation directly against real FRED data) converged on the same measured answer: 3-4 months - roughly twice the summed-stages estimate. The connector-equipped run's summed-stages figure was a reasonable engineering approximation but materially understated the real, measured relationship.

FIX: when a question asks for a specific measured lead/lag time between two economic or physical series (not 'how does the process work' but 'how long, measured'), search specifically for a fitted correlation/lag study (academic, Fed/agency research) OR compute the lag directly yourself if both series are available (a lagged correlation or cross-correlation across a range of lags, checking which lag maximizes the relationship) before settling for a summed-stages estimate. If only a summed-stages estimate is achievable, say so explicitly and flag that it is an engineering approximation that may differ from the true measured lag, rather than presenting it as if it were the fitted answer.

recipes.title: A multi-year or multi-decade dollar-denominated federal figure (grant size, budget, spending) needs a price deflator applied before its trend is reported as the headline finding
recipes.body:
A question comparing a dollar-denominated federal figure across a span of multiple years - a decade or more especially - is easy to answer with the nominal dollar trend, because that is what's directly in the source data and it always shows a bigger number in the later year. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is reporting that nominal growth as the headline finding without checking how much of it is just price inflation.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking whether federal research grants are getting bigger or more numerous, three of four independently-run arms reported nominal award-size growth (roughly +43% to +143% over the multi-decade window) as the headline trend. Only one run deflated the same NIH series using NIH's own BRDPI (Biomedical Research and Development Price Index, a sector-specific deflator, not general CPI) and found the real growth was only +2.2% over the same span, with the constant-dollar figure actually peaking around 2003-2005 and declining since - an order-of-magnitude difference in the conclusion depending on whether inflation is removed.

FIX: when comparing a dollar-denominated federal figure across a span of multiple years, check for and apply the relevant price deflator before reporting the trend as the headline finding. A sector-specific deflator (e.g. NIH's own BRDPI for biomedical research, not general CPI) is preferable when the agency publishes one, since research costs (personnel, equipment, clinical trials) can inflate faster or slower than consumer prices. Report both the nominal and real figures when space allows - the gap between them is itself informative about how much of an apparent trend is real change versus price inflation.

recipes.title: A headline statistic from a domain you don't recognize as an established outlet, that itself returns an error on direct fetch, should be treated as unverifiable rather than cited as fact
recipes.body:
A search result surfacing a precise, headline-ready statistic from an unfamiliar domain is easy to cite directly, because the number looks authoritative and answers the question cleanly. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is trusting the search snippet's framing without checking whether the source itself is retrievable or credible.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question about clinical-trial results-reporting rates by sponsor, three of four arms independently encountered the same specific source (a sponsor-compliance figure from a domain that returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch and reads as AI-generated/non-peer-reviewed). Two arms explicitly flagged and excluded it from their headline figures; one arm used its numbers as a primary cited figure without the same scrutiny.

FIX: when a search result surfaces a headline statistic from a domain you don't recognize as an established outlet, and the page itself returns an HTTP error (403, paywall, bot-block) on direct fetch, treat the figure as unverifiable rather than citing it as fact - even if the search snippet or summary looked authoritative. Prefer using it only where an independent, verifiable source (peer-reviewed literature, a primary regulatory release) corroborates the same number. A precise-looking percentage from an unfetchable source is not more trustworthy for being precise.

recipes.title: A KNOWN official/government page that returns 403 on direct fetch is a bot-block, not evidence the data is unreliable - try a Wayback Machine snapshot before falling back to secondary sources
recipes.body:
This is the mirror-image situation to 'unfetchable-source-is-unverifiable' (an UNFAMILIAR domain returning 403 is a reason to distrust the figure). A 403 from a KNOWN official government or agency source (bls.gov, cdc.gov, census.gov, fda.gov, and similar) almost always means bot-blocking at the edge, not that the underlying data is unreliable or withdrawn - the agency published the page, it just won't serve it to an automated fetch. Treating that 403 the same way as an unfamiliar-domain 403 - giving up on the primary source and falling back to secondary aggregators or a weaker proxy computation - throws away a genuine primary source that is very likely still retrievable another way.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking how workplace fatality rates differ by state and industry, all four arms independently hit the identical HTTP 403 fetching BLS's state x industry cross-tab (bls.gov/iif/state-data/fatal-injury-rates-by-state-and-industry-2023.htm) directly. Three arms treated the 403 as a dead end and fell back to inferring the cross-tab from two separate marginal tables (state-only, industry-only) or a mix-share proxy computed from a different corpus table - correctly labeled as inference, but a materially weaker evidentiary chain. The fourth arm instead retried the same URL through web.archive.org, recovered the actual published cross-tab from a Wayback Machine snapshot, and ran real quantitative analysis (correlations, top-10 combinations) directly on the real data the other three arms only approximated.

FIX: when a fetch to a page on a KNOWN official government/agency domain returns 403 (or another bot-block-shaped error) while a search result or citation confirms the page exists and is the right primary source, do not immediately fall back to secondary aggregators or a proxy computation. First retry the same URL through the Wayback Machine (https://web.archive.org/web/2024/<original-url>, or search web.archive.org for the page) - official pages are frequently crawled and snapshotted, and a snapshot serves the real published data without the live bot-block. Only fall back to inference from marginal tables or a proxy computation if no usable snapshot can be found, and say so explicitly when that's the reason.

recipes.title: On a contested or controversial-topic question with a pullable primary dataset, compute at least one original correlation against the current full population before finalizing an answer built from published regression literature
recipes.body:
A contested-topic question with a body of published regression/comparative-tier literature is easy to answer by synthesizing that literature, because the studies already report clean, dramatic-sounding effect sizes. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is trusting those figures at face value without checking whether they hold up against the raw, current, full population - published studies often report ADJUSTED or CONDITIONAL effects (controlling for confounds, using older or narrower cohorts) that can read as far more dramatic than the unconditional relationship in today's full dataset.

Measured directly in this harness: on a contested question asking how much nursing-home inspection problems track understaffing, three of four arms synthesized published literature reporting strong, dramatic-sounding relationships without any arm computing an original correlation against the full current population to check whether those figures hold up at raw scale. The one arm that did - downloading CMS's own current full provider-level dataset (14,683 facilities) and computing Pearson r directly - found a real but weak relationship (r=-0.20, ~4% of variance), roughly half what the literature's framing implied, and weaker still once ownership was controlled.

FIX: when a contested or controversial-topic question has both a body of published regression/comparative-tier literature and a primary dataset that is realistically pullable in one session, compute at least one original correlation or comparison against the current full population before finalizing the answer - even a simple, unadjusted statistic. It serves as a reality check against literature figures that may be conditional on controls, cohort-specific, or from an older vintage, and the size of any gap between the literature's framing and the raw current relationship is itself often the most newsworthy finding for this kind of accountability question.

recipes.title: When a widely-cited government statistic has a known 'as of' date that predates the question, pull the source agency's own current API directly and construct an explicitly bounded corroborating estimate rather than reporting the stale figure as current
recipes.body:
A widely-cited government or NGO statistic often carries a fixed 'as of' date from whenever the underlying study or report was published, and it is easy to keep citing that same figure verbatim on a later question, because it is well-sourced and already has the right shape for the answer. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is either reporting the stale figure as if it were still current, or refusing to update it at all because a fresher primary computation feels out of scope.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking how concentrated federal flood claims are in repeatedly-flooded properties, the headline literature figure was frozen at a December 2021 snapshot. The most rigorous arm instead ran a live query against the source agency's own current API on the day of the question, returning an exact, reconciled current count and constructing its own explicitly bounded, clearly-labeled corroborating estimate rather than either extreme. This is the second time in this session an arm has done exactly this kind of live-primary-source verification against a stale secondary figure (cf. the NSF HERD reconciliation check), which is why it is now a named recipe rather than a one-off observation.

FIX: when a widely-cited statistic in the literature carries a known 'as of' date that predates the question, check whether the source agency's own API or data portal can be queried live. If so, pull it directly and construct an explicitly bounded, clearly-labeled corroborating estimate rather than either reporting the stale figure as current or declining to update it. Label the live figure and the literature figure distinctly so the reader can see which is which and why they may differ.

recipes.title: A question asking whether gaining some status or position CAUSES an outcome, when units that have the status differ systematically from units that don't
recipes.body:
A question of the shape 'does holding position/status X cause outcome Y' cannot be answered by comparing units that currently have X against units that don't - powerful legislators sit on major committees AND attract more money for reasons that have nothing to do with the committee; systemically-important banks get both a SIFI label and more regulatory attention because they were already large. A cross-sectional comparison bakes in that selection and reports it as an effect of X itself, which is exactly the confound the question is usually built to test for.

The fix is a within-unit design, not a bigger control set: find units whose status CHANGED during the observed window (gained or lost X for reasons that are at least plausibly unrelated to Y - a chamber-control flip reshuffling committee ratios, a term-limited chair rotating off, a seniority-queue vacancy fill, a size threshold crossed by an unrelated event), then compare each such unit's own outcome before vs. after the change against a matched control group of similar units (same party, similar seniority/size/sector) whose status did NOT change over the same window. Run this as panel_fixed_effects or diff_in_diff with the status as the treatment indicator, entity and time both absorbed as fixed effects - not a single cross-sectional regression with status as one more covariate. Then run event_study on the same panel and check the PRE-treatment period coefficients are jointly not significantly different from zero before trusting the post-treatment ones: if the outcome was already trending differently for soon-to-be-treated units before the status change actually happened, that is selection revealing itself, not the treatment effect, and no amount of control-variable-adding fixes it.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking whether industries concentrate contributions on legislators sitting on the committee that regulates them, an arm working from a public-data connector could not build this design end-to-end in one session (no committee-assignment history table was available) but independently proposed the exact identification strategy - a committee-reassignment natural experiment with member-level before/after comparison against same-seniority controls - as the design that WOULD separate 'contributions follow jurisdiction' from 'jurisdiction follows prior alignment'. A companion arm working from published literature found that this design had already been run: Fouirnaies & Hall (2018, AJPS) use exactly this within-legislator committee-assignment-change design across 99 state legislative chambers and find a real premium (~32% average) for industries under a committee's jurisdiction once the seat change itself is the identifying event - while their own built-in placebo test (donors from industries with NO jurisdictional relationship to the committee) shows no comparable jump, confirming the design actually isolates the targeted effect rather than a generic 'new committee seat, more money of all kinds' story.

FIX: whenever a question asks about the causal effect of gaining or holding a status/position/designation, first check whether ANY units changed status during the covered window. If none did, say so plainly and fall back to a cross-sectional comparison labeled as correlational, not causal. If some did, build the within-unit before/after panel against matched non-changing controls, run panel_fixed_effects/diff_in_diff for the effect and event_study for the pre-trend check, and report the pre-trend result alongside the effect size - a significant post-period effect with a clean (non-significant) pre-trend is real evidence; either result without the pre-trend check reported is not. Generalizes past committee assignments to any status-gain-or-loss question: SIFI/systemically-important designation, Opportunity Zone status, rural-hospital or critical-access designation, right-to-work adoption, a firm crossing a regulatory size threshold, a county gaining or losing a disaster declaration.

recipes.title: Sorting or filtering sec.filing_contexts by period_instant to find the MOST RECENT context silently drops or buries every duration-type context
recipes.body:
sec.filing_contexts carries BOTH point-in-time (instant, e.g. a balance-sheet date) and duration (a reporting period, e.g. a quarter) contexts in the same table, and only ONE of period_instant / (period_start, period_end) is ever populated per row depending on which kind of fact the context describes - a duration context's period_instant is NULL. Most dimensional segment breakdowns (a loan-class disclosure, a business-segment table, anything reported 'for the three months ended') are DURATION contexts, not instant ones. Sorting or filtering the table by period_instant alone to find 'the most recent' row for a filer/segment therefore treats every duration-context row as having no date at all - and DuckDB sorts NULL first on DESC, so an ORDER BY period_instant DESC LIMIT-style query surfaces old rows (or nothing useful) while the actual newest filing's duration contexts sit invisibly at the bottom, with no error and no empty result to signal the mistake.

Measured directly in this harness: an askamerica arm joined filing_contexts to a company's CommercialRealEstatePortfolioSegmentMember dimension with ORDER BY period_instant DESC and concluded the loaded segment data 'stops at fiscal year-end 2019', falling back to an external press-release figure instead of computing the company's own current-quarter ratio from the corpus. The connector in fact held the identical current-year 10-Q the external figure came from - an instant-type context for that same segment WAS present at the correct date, but it never surfaced because the query's sort silently buried every duration-type context (the segment's actual quarterly disclosures) beneath it. The gap was not in the data; it was in the query shape.

FIX: never sort or filter a mixed instant/duration context set by period_instant alone. Use COALESCE(period_instant, period_end) as the recency key, or filter on period_end specifically when the target concept is known to be a duration fact (most segment/dimensional breakdowns are). Before concluding a filer's or segment's data 'stops' at some date, run an unordered MAX(accession_number) (or MAX(filing_date)) check for that cik/segment first - a sort-order artifact produces a false 'stops early' conclusion with no error, while a real coverage gap will still show the same stale max under the unordered check.

recipes.title: A top-N ranking whose values sit within a few points of each other needs a real significance test, not just a reported margin of error
recipes.body:
Reporting a margin of error next to a point estimate is not the same as testing whether a ranking is real. A question that asks 'which state/entity ranks highest' and turns up several candidates within a few points of each other needs an actual test of whether the gap between the top candidates exceeds what sampling noise alone would produce - not just naming each one's own MOE and moving on, and not silently picking whichever value happens to be numerically largest.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking which state's household income grew the most and whether that survives a cost-of-living adjustment, one arm reported its top state's own margin of error (well under 2% of the point estimate) and treated the ranking as settled at that point - its top-3 states sat within a 2.2-point spread of each other, and that spread was never tested against the combined sampling error of the states being compared. A second, unaided arm working the same question by hand recognized the top-2 states' gap (about 0.04 points) was inside the ACS/CPS standard errors and explicitly reported it as a statistical tie rather than naming a single winner - the correct call, reached without any connector tools at all, on a question the connector-equipped arm had the tools to settle more rigorously and did not.

FIX: whenever a ranking's top few values sit within roughly the combined margin of error of each other, do not stop at reporting each value's own MOE - run hypothesis_test (or a two-sample comparison via the appropriate statistical tool) on the top candidates' difference to check whether it is actually distinguishable from zero. If it is not, say so as a tie or a statistical toss-up and name which candidates are functionally indistinguishable, rather than reporting a single winner the data cannot actually support. This applies to any close top-N comparison across states, industries, institutions, or time periods - not just income growth.

recipes.title: A missing OR wrong connector answer isn't a stopping point — fetch the source agency's own primary data externally before settling for a caveated bad number or literature synthesis, the way a fully-resourced analyst would
triggers: how has X changed over the last N years
no table for this in the corpus
every row has the same sign
narrower population than the question asks
covers a subset of the true total
recipes.body:
A confirmed connector coverage gap OR a confirmed WRONG answer from a table that does exist (a sanity check against a known landmark figure fails, e.g. a 'donor state' computation that shows every single state as a net beneficiary, or a total that is off by a multiple from a published aggregate) is not the end of the analysis - it means switch to WebSearch/WebFetch and get the SAME primary data a fully-resourced analyst (this harness's 'expert' persona, with a full shell, filesystem, and Python) would get, rather than settling for secondary literature synthesis as if that were the ceiling of what's achievable.

Measured directly in this harness, twice: (1) on a calendar-anchored FDA drug-review-time question, the arm that stopped at literature synthesis (era medians from industry commentary) got a materially less precise answer than the arm that instead fetched FDA's own primary per-application dataset directly from fda.gov and bucketed it into the exact calendar windows asked about. (2) On separate questions, the 'expert' persona routinely out-performs by extracting a primary source's own published table directly - a PDF report via pdfplumber, or a government agency's compiled Excel workbook - rather than relaying what secondary web coverage says about that source.

FIX: when a connector table is confirmed absent or insufficient for a question, before writing an answer based on literature synthesis, spend one real attempt trying to fetch the source agency's own primary dataset directly (a .csv/.xlsx download, a public API, a data portal) via WebFetch. A fetched primary file may arrive as raw text/bytes this connector cannot parse as a spreadsheet or PDF table (no Python tool is available here, unlike a real Claude Desktop session) - if so, say exactly that ('found the primary source at <url> but cannot parse its .xlsx/PDF table without a code-execution tool') rather than silently falling back to a paraphrased secondary figure without naming what was actually available. Only settle for literature synthesis, clearly labeled as an approximation, once a genuine primary-source fetch has been attempted and specifically could not be used.

A WRONG answer deserves the exact same external-fallback response as a MISSING one, not a lesser one: report the wrong figure with a caveat, or stop at 'this table can't answer it.' Measured directly in this harness: on a federal-money-vs-taxes-paid-by-state question, a table pairing a state's ALL-source federal spending against its INDIVIDUAL-INCOME-TAX-ONLY revenue made literally every one of 51 states/DC look like a net beneficiary, including California and New York - which every independent published analysis identifies as the largest net PAYERS. The correct response, and the one taken, was not to report this internal number with a caveat, but to name the exact mechanism of the error precisely (a 2.2x base mismatch, ~$4.66T vs ~$2.10T nationally) and switch to Rockefeller Institute/USAFacts external data for the actual headline figures - the defect is worth reporting IN ADDITION to answering the question correctly, never INSTEAD of it.

A THIRD shape, distinct from missing/wrong: a connector table returns a PLAUSIBLE number that is honestly caveated as covering a narrower population than the question actually asks about - this is not a bug and looks responsible, but it is still the same 'settled for less than a fully-resourced analyst would get' failure if a broader-population primary source was available and not fetched. Measured directly in this harness on a federal-research-funding-by-field question: the connector's only field-of-R&D table (`research.nsf_herd_by_institution`, NSF HERD survey) covers federal money that funds research performed AT UNIVERSITIES only - a real but narrower slice of total federal research, excluding DOD's much larger contractor/intramural R&D. The run correctly disclosed this scope limit and even correctly noted the table's declared date range (2008-2024) actually held no data before 2010, but then filled the pre-2010 gap with qualitative literature synthesis instead of fetching AAAS's own compiled 'Historical Data.xlsx' (aaas.org/programs/r-d-budget-and-policy), sourced from the SAME NCSES Survey of Federal Funds for R&D that covers the true ALL-agency, ALL-performer federal research total across the full 20-year window - a file this harness's 'expert' persona fetched directly in the same comparative run and used to build a complete, cross-validated 21-year series. Naming the scope caveat is necessary but not sufficient: FIX is the same as above - attempt a primary-source fetch for the broader population BEFORE settling for a caveated narrower-population answer plus literature fill-in, and only fall back to the narrower table (clearly labeled as such) if that fetch genuinely fails.

recipes.title: No single clean government series measures industry-level import penetration over a long window — substitute and disclose, don't force one source
recipes.body:
There is no single, freely-queryable, industry-level import-penetration series spanning a long (e.g. 20-year) window. The two natural government sources are both blocked in different ways: Census's international trade API requires a key with no self-service path in this connector's reach, and BEA's Import Matrix / apparent-consumption tables are published as an interactive web tool, not a downloadable series. Expect one of these substitutions instead, and name which one was used rather than presenting it as the literal thing asked for:

  1. Compute your own penetration ratio by joining econ.industry_gdp (BEA Gross Output, domestic production) against econ.trade_imports/trade_exports (Census HS, at whatever industry crosswalk grain both sides support) - this is reproducible from data already in the warehouse but the earliest usable year may be much later than the requested window's start (Census HS detail in this warehouse currently starts around 2013).

  2. Fall back to BEA end-use trade categories (capital goods, industrial supplies, consumer goods, etc.) - coarser than a true industry breakdown but freely available for the full requested window.

  3. Cite an academic paper that used confidential Census microdata to compute true NAICS-level penetration (e.g. Amiti & Heise, NY Fed) - precise industry detail, but on whatever window that paper's authors happened to study, not the window the question asks about.

A trade-share-of-GDP or trade-balance figure is NOT the same measurement as import penetration and can move in the opposite direction: manufactured-goods import SHARE OF TRADE can fall even as true import PENETRATION (imports / (imports + domestic production - exports)) rises, if domestic output is growing slower than both imports and exports. Compute penetration directly rather than inferring it from a trade-balance or trade-share trend.

recipes.title: A press/colloquial name for a farm-payment program (e.g. "Farmer Bridge Assistance") often differs from its official USDA program_description
recipes.body:
A question naming a farm trade-war compensation program by its press/colloquial name (e.g. "Farmer Bridge Assistance" for the 2025-26 round) will not necessarily match anything in search_catalog or in a table name search - the official USDA FSA program_description used inside ag.fsa_commodity_payments is often a different, more bureaucratic name than what news coverage calls it. Measured directly in this harness: the actual 2025 disbursements for the currently-active round appear under program_description = 'EMERGENCY COMMODITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM' ($9.36B in 2025), not under any table or program name matching "Farmer Bridge Assistance" - an agent that searched for the press name and found nothing incorrectly concluded no data existed for the current round.

Before concluding a named farm-payment program has no data in the corpus: query `SELECT DISTINCT program_description FROM ag.fsa_commodity_payments WHERE "year" >= <most recent 1-2 years>` and scan the returned list for a plausible official-name match, rather than relying on search_catalog or a table-name search finding the press name directly. This applies generally whenever a question names an event or program colloquially (an informal or press shorthand) rather than by its official government designation - check the underlying table's own category/program values for the current period before concluding the program isn't covered.

Also, when a question names an ambiguous or unscoped event ("the trade war", not a specific year), and the domain has more than one live or recent episode as of the question's own date, address ALL currently-relevant episodes rather than only the most historically-documented one - a still-actively-disbursing current-year program is at least as relevant as a well-documented older one, and skipping it is a real completeness gap even if the older episode is answered thoroughly.

recipes.title: Two different-looking percentages for the same phenomenon may be the same study's gross and net estimate, not literature disagreement
recipes.body:
When two different percentages circulate for what looks like the same underlying phenomenon (e.g. bank branch closures causing a '9-13%' lending decline in one citation and a '19%' decline in another), do not assume this is genuine disagreement between two separate studies before checking whether they are actually the SAME paper's gross and net estimates.

Measured directly in this harness: a bank-branch-closure lending study's commonly cited '9-13%' and '19%' figures are the same paper's gross-vs-net decomposition, not two competing findings - a 19% GROSS decline in the directly-affected lender's activity shrinks to roughly 10% NET once other lenders (smaller banks, credit unions) absorb about half the gap. Reporting either number alone, or treating both as competing estimates from different sources, misses the actual finding: the effect is real but partially self-healing, and a reader needs the residual/net figure to correctly size the uncompensated harm, not the gross figure that ignores substitution.

Before presenting two circulating figures for the same effect as a range or as competing estimates: check the primary source(s) directly for whether one is a gross effect and the other a net-of-substitution effect from the identical study, or whether a headline figure and a footnoted adjusted figure are being separately cited. If so, report both explicitly labeled (gross vs. net, before vs. after substitution) rather than either picking one or presenting the pair as an unresolved range.

Separately: a specific circulating statistic that cannot be traced to a named, identifiable publication (only to a source category like 'one study' or 'researchers found') should be omitted from the answer entirely, not repeated with vague attribution - if you cannot find the actual source when checking, say so and drop the figure rather than keep it because it fits the narrative.

recipes.title: Ranking industries or donors by campaign money requires naming the channel: direct PAC contributions (24K) and independent expenditure are separate tables with different leaders, and the independent-expenditure table cannot be summed raw
recipes.body:
A question about which industries, companies or interests "gave the most" to candidates - or whether donors got anything for it - has to state WHICH CHANNEL it measured, because federal money reaches a candidate through several and the warehouse holds them in separate tables. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is to sum direct PAC contributions (fec.committee_contributions, transaction_type='24K'), group them by fec.committees.connected_org_name, and present the result as industry giving. That is a real and defensible measure of direct contributions, but it is not total industry spending, and for some cycles the two rankings barely overlap.

Measured directly in this harness (q3, 2026-09-02): a run built industry buckets exactly that way for the 2023-2024 cycle and ranked LABOR UNIONS first at $22.2M to winning candidates, with no crypto industry anywhere in its table. Three independently-run unaided arms on the same question all led with CRYPTO. Neither side was hallucinating - crypto's 2024 money ran almost entirely through non-connected super PACs (Fairshake and allies), which never appear in 24K contribution rows. The run reported its ranking without noting the channel restriction, so the divergence from every published account of that cycle went unexplained.

FIX, in three parts.

1. SIZE WHAT connected_org_name GROUPING DROPS. Group the cycle's 24K rows by connected_org_name and look at the 'NONE' bucket before trusting any industry ranking built on the named ones. In the 2023-2024 cycle that bucket totals $118.2M - roughly ten times the largest single named organisation (National Association of Realtors, $12.6M). Non-connected and leadership PACs carry no connected_org_name, so an industry table assembled from named committees alone is a minority of the dollars.

2. QUERY THE OTHER CHANNEL - IT IS IN THE WAREHOUSE. fec.independent_expenditures holds independent expenditure by spender_name, election_year, support_oppose ('S' support / 'O' oppose), candidate_id and amount. fec.electioneering_communications and fec.communication_costs cover two further channels. Do not conclude the outside-spending channel is unavailable without checking these; on q3 it was never queried and the omission drove the whole divergence above.

3. NEVER SUM fec.independent_expenditures RAW - IT IS FILER-SUBMITTED AND UNVALIDATED. FEC publishes these rows as filed, and junk filings dominate any naive total. Verified in this harness: for election_year 2024, support_oppose='S', the top spender_name by summed amount is 'THE COMMITTEE OF 300' at $26.7 BILLION across THREE rows, one of them a single $9.78B line, followed by 'THE COURT OF DIVINE JUSTICE' ($10.0B), 'Republican Emo Girl' ($6.3B) and 'The Masonic Illuminati Eye' ($580M). None is an amendment artifact - all carry amendment_indicator='N'. Real total federal independent expenditure for the 2024 cycle was roughly $4.5B across ALL committees, so any single spender above that is impossible on its face. The genuine large spenders sit below the junk: Americans for Prosperity Action ($108M), America PAC ($105M), SFA Fund ($64M). Before using this table, bound or drop implausible rows and sanity-check the total against a known cycle aggregate; report the filter you applied.

Whatever you end up measuring, say so in the answer - 'direct PAC contributions to winning candidates' and 'total industry election spending' are different quantities with different leaders, and a ranking that does not name its channel will be read as the second when it is the first. Related: see verify-the-population-before-answering-the-famous-subset for the adjacent case where the population itself, rather than the channel, is the narrowed thing.

recipes.title: A null against one outcome is not a null against the policy — and a comparison question naming two subjects needs BOTH tested, not one with the other disclosed as a scope gap
triggers: only covers one of the two
recipes.body:
When a question asks whether some policy or characteristic produced better results, it usually names or implies MORE THAN ONE outcome — income growth, cost-of-living-adjusted wages, migration, employment. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is to pick the single most obvious outcome, find no relationship, and report a null as if it settled the question. It does not. The same predictor can be flat against one outcome and strongly related to another, and the outcome you skipped may be the one carrying the actual answer.

Measured directly in this harness (q7, 2026-09-02, a question about whether states did better for household incomes by investing or by keeping taxes low). One run tested state tax burden and a public-investment index against real median household income growth alone, found r=0.05 (p=0.71) and r=-0.10 (p=0.49), and correctly reported a rigorous null. A second run on the identical question tested the same levers against THREE outcomes and found near-zero against income growth (r=0.05 tax rank, r=-0.08 education spend) but STRONGLY negative against net domestic migration (r=-0.51 and r=-0.61). Low-tax states had not grown incomes faster; they had gained PEOPLE. The single-outcome run's null was correct for what it tested and was not the answer to the question asked.

A sibling failure, same root cause: a question that explicitly names TWO SUBJECTS to compare (not two outcomes for one subject) and only one gets analyzed, with the other disclosed as a scope limitation rather than attempted. Measured directly in this harness (q54, 2026-09-22): asked whether speculative positioning in energy futures leads, lags, or moves with production 'and does the relationship differ between crude and natural gas', a run built a real weekly panel and multi-lag cross-correlation test for WTI crude only, explicitly stating the natural-gas half was out of scope — while a comparison answer built the identical analysis for BOTH crude and Henry Hub natural gas using the same corpus (CFTC positioning by commodity code, EIA storage tables for both), directly answering the crude-vs-gas comparison the question was built to test. The crude-only analysis was itself high quality; the gap was stopping at one of the two named subjects instead of the whole comparison.

FIX: before reporting a scope limitation on a named second outcome OR a named second comparison subject, check whether the corpus holds (or plausibly holds, by analogy to a table already found for the first one) an equivalent table for it — a second commodity's futures-positioning code, a second outcome's own government-finance table, a second category's own aggregate. Report the full outcome-by-predictor grid, or the full per-subject comparison, including cells that came back null, rather than the single cell or subject you tested. Where the predictor or relationship behaves differently across outcomes or subjects, THAT divergence is the finding and should lead the answer — and for a comparison question specifically, an honestly-disclosed 'I only covered one side' is a materially weaker answer than a same-quality analysis of both sides, not an acceptable substitute for it.

Related but different: the-unit-of-aggregation-is-a-choice-that-changes-the-answer covers varying the GRAIN of a series (a narrow industry code versus the broader category containing it). This recipe covers varying the OUTCOME VARIABLE, or the COMPARISON SUBJECT, at a fixed grain. All are cases of one test not being the test, but they move along different axes and a question can need more than one.

recipes.title: Dropping years, units or outliers from an aggregate obliges you to report the delta — run it both ways and state what the exclusion moved
triggers: trend over the last ten years
recipes.body:
Filtering an aggregate is often correct — a year whose reporting coverage collapsed, a city-state that is not comparable to states, a table-year loaded only in part. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is to state the exclusion as a methodology note and move on, leaving the reader unable to tell whether it moved the answer by a rounding error or by a third of the effect. An exclusion you cannot price is indistinguishable from a choice that produced the result you reported.

Measured directly in this harness. On a 2026-09-02 crime question a run excluded 31 of 510 state-years whose FBI reporting coverage fell below 80% - a correct and well-justified filter, reported as a methodology line with no quantification. Checking the cost directly: Alaska's ten-year mean violent-crime rate is 783 per 100k computed over all ten years and 805 once the low-coverage state-years are dropped, a 22-point swing on a single state, and the direction is systematic rather than random - the filter always removes under-reported years, so it always raises the affected state's average and flattens the spread between extremes. A separate run on a health question excluded a whole year on the same reasoning and likewise never reported what the exclusion changed.

FIX: whenever you drop years, units, or outliers from an aggregate, compute the aggregate BOTH ways and report the delta in the answer, not only the filter. One extra query - the same aggregate with the WHERE clause removed - is enough. Say which direction the exclusion pushes and whether it is systematic (a coverage filter always removes under-reported periods, so it has a sign) or incidental. If the delta is negligible, saying so strengthens the result; if it is large, the reader needed to know and the exclusion is itself part of the finding. This applies equally to dropping DC from a state comparison, which several analyses in this corpus do by convention - state the convention AND its effect on the headline number.

Detecting WHICH periods to exclude in the crime series specifically is covered by crime-series-reporting-coverage-instability; this recipe is about what you owe the reader once you have excluded anything, in any table.

SQL SHAPES THAT ARE EXCLUSIONS (measured 2026-09-10, q134): appending `AND avg_frpl_rate IS NOT NULL AND jurisdiction_name <> 'District of Columbia'` to a 51-jurisdiction state query before ols_regression turned it into a 45-unit regression, and the answer said "45 states" without naming DC or the five null-FRPL states it removed, or what removing them changed. `<> '<name>'`, `NOT IN (...)` and `IS NOT NULL` on a covariate are all exclusions in this sense. The server now returns an `explicit_exclusion` diagnostic on such SQL and a `sample_attrition` diagnostic naming rows dropped for null (`rows_dropped_examples` in the stats payload): when either appears, list the units in the answer and report the headline with and without them.

recipes.title: A before/after comparison around a dated policy event, where the baseline window was picked rather than derived
triggers: before and after the tax cut
did the policy move the trend
recipes.body:
Asking whether a rate of change moved after a dated policy event forces a choice the data does not make for you: how far back the 'before' window reaches. That choice is not cosmetic - on a series with any curvature it can decide the answer, and an asymmetric pre/post pair can manufacture flatness or acceleration out of the same rows.

Measured directly in this harness. Asked whether ordinary workers' pay rose after the 2017 corporate tax cut, a run computed real average hourly earnings for production/nonsupervisory workers from econ.wage_growth (CES0500000008) deflated by econ.inflation_metrics (CUUR0000SA0) and reported 1.11%/yr before against 1.11%/yr after - headline: 'no acceleration at all'. The arithmetic was exact. But the 'before' was 2014-2017 (three years) and the 'after' was 2017-2019 (two), and the answer described BOTH as two years. Recomputed like-for-like on two-year windows the same table gives 0.685% -> 1.113%, which reads as acceleration. Nothing was wrong with the data or the code; the conclusion was an artifact of an unjustified, mislabelled window. A second unaided analyst on the same question avoided this by reporting two different wage measures that disagreed in direction and concluding only that there was no visible break at the effective date - a claim that survives the window choice.

FIX, before publishing any before/after comparison:
(1) Make the pre and post windows the SAME length and say what that length is. If the post-period is short because the policy is recent, shorten the pre-period to match rather than reaching back for a longer, better-looking baseline.
(2) Recompute on at least one alternative pre-window - one year shorter and one year longer is enough - before deciding what the headline says. In this corpus that is one more GROUP BY year against a table you have already queried, so the check is nearly free.
