Note that several econ tables DECLARE a narrower range than they hold (econ.wage_growth declares 2018-2024 and holds 2009-2026 measured), so run data_coverage or a MIN/MAX year scan rather than assuming a short declared window forbids the baseline you need.
(3) If the sign or the headline changes across those windows, that sensitivity IS the finding - report both and say the conclusion is window-dependent. Do not pick the window whose result reads more cleanly.
(4) Prefer a claim that does not rest on one window at all where the data allows it: whether there is a visible break at the effective date, or whether two independent measures of the same quantity agree in direction, both survive a reader disagreeing with your baseline choice.

This is about CHOOSING a baseline window, not about disclosing rows you removed - for the latter see report-what-an-exclusion-changed-not-only-that-you-made-one. Where the event admits a real control group, a diff_in_diff or event_study on a panel is stronger than any single-series before/after and should be preferred; this recipe is the floor for when only one series exists.

recipes.title: Measuring the effect of a STATE policy change, when the corpus can build genuine border-county control pairs
triggers: what happened in the state next door
employment effect of a state law
policy change at the state line
recipes.body:
When a question asks what a STATE policy change did to a local outcome, the default reach is a state panel - log(outcome) on log(policy) with state and year fixed effects across all 50 states. That design is publishable and often correct, but it compares states to other states, so every difference in regional economic trajectory rides along inside the estimate. The literature's answer to that problem is the ADJACENT CROSS-STATE COUNTY PAIR: compare a county on one side of a state line to the county it physically touches on the other side. The pair shares a labour market, a weather shock, a commuting zone and a regional business cycle; what it does not share is the state law. That is the whole point, and it is why border-pair estimates are treated as the more credible identification in this literature (Dube, Lester & Reich; the Allegretto-Dube-Reich-Zipperer side of the long dispute with Neumark, Salas & Wascher).

THIS CORPUS CAN BUILD THAT DESIGN DIRECTLY, and callers do not know it. The three tables:
  - geo.county_adjacency - the real Census Bureau County Adjacency File. Columns county_fips, state_fips, neighbor_county_fips, neighbor_state_fips. Filter state_fips <> neighbor_state_fips and you have the border-pair sample frame: verified 7,848 cross-state adjacent pairs across 1,184 border counties.
  - econ.county_qcew - BLS QCEW at county x NAICS industry_code x own_code x year, carrying annual_avg_emplvl AND total_annual_wages, so both the employment count and the WAGE BILL are answerable. Verified ~3,250 counties in every year from 2008 to 2025 for industry_code='722' (food service), own_code='5' (private).
  - the policy timing table for the change itself - e.g. fiscal.state_minimum_wage_history.
Joining adjacency to county_qcew on both sides returns 18,114 matched treated/neighbour observations. This is one query, not a project.

Measured in this harness: asked what happens to low-wage jobs after a state raises its minimum wage, a run produced a careful two-way fixed-effects state panel plus an event study - good work, correctly caveated - while all three tables above sat available, and search_catalog had returned econ.county_qcew and econ.county_wages on the SAME first page as econ.state_wages. The answer even cited the border-county-versus-state-panel dispute by name before choosing the state panel. Separately, an unaided analyst on the same question reached for cross-state county comparison on its own and could only manage two pairs by hand, saying explicitly that the full sweep was out of scope - which is exactly the work this join removes.

THE PLAUSIBLE-BUT-WRONG SHORTCUT, name it and avoid it: picking two geographically distant counties in different states and calling it a county-pair design. That same unaided run paired Maricopa County AZ against Salt Lake County UT, and King County WA against Ada County ID - hundreds of miles apart in each case. Those are two counties, not a border pair, and they buy none of the shared-local-shock control the design exists for. If you are not joining through an adjacency table, you are not running this design.

HOW TO RUN IT: build the pair set from geo.county_adjacency where the two sides are in different states; attach the outcome from econ.county_qcew for both members at the same year and the same industry_code; difference within pair (or include pair fixed effects); and CLUSTER ON THE PAIR, or on the border segment, not on the state - counties within a pair are not independent observations. Report the pair count and how many pairs survive the industry and year filters, because coverage thins at small counties. Where treatment timing is staggered across several years, the staggered-adoption caution still applies (see assignment-change-natural-experiment) - restricting comparisons to never-treated neighbours is the cheap mitigation.

WHEN NOT TO USE IT: if the question is explicitly about a state aggregate ('how did the STATE do'), the state panel answers what was asked and this design answers something narrower - say which one you ran and why. Border counties are also not a random sample of the country: they are more rural and less dense than interior counties, so a border-pair estimate is internally credible and externally narrower. State that trade-off rather than presenting the pair estimate as the national number.

Related: the-unit-of-aggregation-is-a-choice-that-changes-the-answer covers choosing among sibling tables at different grains and what to do when the needed grain is absent; this recipe is the case where the finer grain is present AND unlocks a specific quasi-experimental design through a join the caller would not think to look for.

recipes.title: Aggregating a long/tidy survey table whose single value column stacks different units, practices, statistics and geography levels
recipes.body:
Some tables in this corpus are long/tidy mirrors of a survey API - one generic `value` column, with every other column acting as a qualifier that says what that value MEANS. ag.nass_crop_production (USDA NASS QuickStats) is the canonical one. A single commodity-year in it carries, side by side in the same `value` column:
  - different UNITS - unit_desc of BU, TONS, and $ (dollars). Summing these adds bushels to tons to money.
  - different UTILIZATION - util_practice_desc of GRAIN vs SILAGE. Corn for grain and corn for silage are different crops measured differently.
  - different STATISTICS - statisticcat_desc of PRODUCTION, AREA HARVESTED, AREA PLANTED, YIELD.
  - NESTED GEOGRAPHY - agg_level_desc of COUNTY and STATE in the same result set, so county rows are double-counted inside their own state totals.
Measured directly in this harness on corn, 2023: 406 GRAIN/BU/COUNTY rows, 46 SILAGE/TONS/COUNTY, 14 SILAGE/TONS/STATE, 12 GRAIN/BU/STATE and 12 GRAIN/$/STATE, all matching a naive `statisticcat_desc LIKE '%production%'` filter.

WHAT GOES WRONG: a run computed national corn yield as SUM(production)/SUM(area harvested) over state rows and got 85 bu/acre for 2023 against a published 177.3. A different naive sum of the same table gave 237.6 for 2018 and 327.6 for 2023 - wrong in the OPPOSITE direction. Three different wrong answers out of one table that is perfectly faithful to its source. The first run correctly recognised its number was implausible and discarded it, which is the right instinct - but it then told the reader the TABLE was unreliable. That conclusion is wrong and it is expensive, because it writes off a good table instead of fixing a query.

FIX - pin every qualifier before any SUM or ratio:
  WHERE commodity_desc = 'CORN'
    AND agg_level_desc = 'STATE'            -- or 'COUNTY', never both
    AND util_practice_desc = 'GRAIN'        -- not SILAGE
    AND unit_desc = 'BU'                    -- excludes the $ rows
    AND statisticcat_desc = 'PRODUCTION'    -- and a matching filter for AREA HARVESTED
Then SANITY-CHECK the aggregate against the published national figure before using it. NASS publishes national corn and soybean yields directly; if your computed number is not within a percent or so of the published one, a qualifier is still unpinned. Prefer the published national when one exists and you only need the total - recompute from rows only when you need a cut the publisher does not offer.

AND WHEN THE CHECK FAILS, SAY WHICH FILTER WAS MISSING, not that the table is untrustworthy. 'Summing across unit_desc mixed bushels with dollars' is actionable; 'this table produced implausible results' sends the next caller to an inferior source for no reason. Run a `SELECT unit_desc, util_practice_desc, agg_level_desc, COUNT(*) GROUP BY 1,2,3` on your own filter before trusting any total from a table of this shape - it takes one query and shows immediately whether you are summing one thing or several.

Related: the-unit-of-aggregation-is-a-choice-that-changes-the-answer covers choosing between SIBLING TABLES that hold the same series at different grains, and what to do when the grain you need does not exist. This recipe is the different problem of one table whose ROWS mix grains and units internally - the fix there is picking the right table, the fix here is constraining the query.

recipes.title: Choosing the grain of an analysis - which unit, what to do when it does not exist, and whether the finding survives the choice
triggers: county stands in for the city
did the policy help this industry
does the finding hold at county level
recipes.body:
Grain is not a retrieval detail, it is a modelling decision, and it fails in three distinct ways. Work them in order; they are not alternatives.

=== 1. IS THERE A SIBLING TABLE AT THE GRAIN THE QUESTION NAMES? ===
This corpus commonly loads the SAME underlying series at multiple grains as separate sibling tables - econ carries state_wages, metro_wages, county_wages AND county_qcew side by side, all from BLS QCEW. search_catalog returns all of them for a generic keyword and ranks them by textual relevance to that keyword, NOT by which grain the question needs, so the first or most obviously-named match is very often the wrong one.
Measured here: a question explicitly requiring adjacent cross-state COUNTY pairs was answered with a state-level two-way-fixed-effects panel. search_catalog's own results for the query used ('minimum wage') had already listed county_qcew and county_wages by name, multiple times, alongside state_wages - the finer tables were surfaced and simply not opened. The analysis was well executed and answered a coarser question than the one asked.
FIX: when a question names or implies a unit (county, metro, congressional district, adjacent/bordering, establishment), scan the FULL search_catalog result for a sibling at that grain before settling on the first match. Prefer the named grain even when it costs more join effort.

=== 2. WHAT IF THE REQUIRED GRAIN IS NOT IN THE CORPUS AT ALL? ===
Sometimes no sibling exists, and then there is nothing to prefer. This is common when the SUBJECT is defined more finely than the statistical program that publishes it: municipal ordinances, school-district policies, city taxes. The corpus loads the Census Building Permits Survey COUNTY file only (housing.building_permits) - there is no place/municipality table - so any question about a CITY housing policy can only be answered with COUNTY permits.
Measured here: asked whether rent control suppresses construction, a run compared Ramsey County against Hennepin County to stand in for St. Paul against Minneapolis, and wrote 'Ramsey County (St. Paul)' as though they were the same object, carrying that onto a chart subtitle as 'Ramsey Co. = St. Paul'. The ordinance binds only inside St. Paul, which is 56% of Ramsey County by population; Minneapolis is only 33% of Hennepin. Both series are diluted by suburbs the policy never touched, biasing the effect toward zero. The numbers were right; the failure was entirely in not saying so.
FIX: analyse at the coarsest grain available - that is the right call, not a reason to refuse - then (a) state plainly that the unit of analysis is coarser than the unit the question is about, naming both, (b) BOUND THE DILUTION with a number: query the treated sub-unit's share of the reporting unit (population shares come from the census schema joined to geo.counties on county_fips; use resolve_geo when the place-to-county mapping is not obvious), and (c) say which way it pushes - a treatment diluted by untreated area biases toward zero, so a surviving effect is conservative and a null is uninformative. NEVER print the fine-grain name in parentheses after the coarse-grain unit, or set the two equal in a chart title.

=== 3. DOES THE FINDING SURVIVE THE GRAIN? (the one most often skipped) ===
Steps 1 and 2 get you the right unit. They do not tell you whether the ANSWER depends on it. For any question about a RELATIONSHIP - a correlation, an elasticity, a regression coefficient, 'does X predict Y', 'did the policy move the outcome' - the result can change magnitude or flip sign purely from the aggregation level. This is the modifiable areal unit problem, and it is not a curiosity; it is the normal case.
Measured here in the INDUSTRY-CODE dimension: a policy targeting steel mills (NAICS 3311) showed +3.3% employment at that code while the broader primary-metals category containing it (NAICS 331, which also holds aluminum and foundries the policy never targeted) showed -2.4% over the identical window and the identical policy action. Same data, same period, opposite signs, chosen entirely by which code you pulled.
The GEOGRAPHIC dimension behaves the same way and is more common. Two mechanisms, and they need different fixes:
  (a) THE VARIABLE STOPS MEASURING WHAT IT IS NAMED. A state's population density is people divided by land area, most of which nobody lives on - Alaska's and Nevada's density describe empty desert and tundra, not where anyone actually lives. A relationship built on that predictor can be weak at state level and strong at county level without anything about the underlying relationship changing. The fix here is often a better-constructed VARIABLE rather than a finer unit: population-weighted density recovers most of what you want at the same grain. (Mechanism, not a harness measurement - this specific pair has not been tested here.)
  (b) AGGREGATION AVERAGES OUT WITHIN-UNIT VARIATION, which changes the correlation. Note the direction is NOT reliably 'coarser is weaker' - the classic result (Robinson 1950) is that ecological correlations usually run LARGER in magnitude than individual-level ones, because averaging removes noise. So do not adopt 'finer is truer' as a rule either.
FINER GRAIN HAS ITS OWN FAILURE MODES, and they bite hardest on exactly the questions that tempt you to it: outcomes are recorded where the event happens while population is counted where people sleep, so any county with net daytime commuting inflow has a corrupted denominator; small counties give unstable rates on small numerators; and disclosure suppression removes cells non-randomly. 'County' is also not one kind of object - Virginia's independent cities, Louisiana's parishes and Alaska's boroughs are not comparable units.
FIX: compute the relationship at TWO grains - the one the question names and the next level up or down - before deciding what the headline says. If sign or magnitude moves, that sensitivity IS the finding: report both and say the conclusion is grain-dependent, rather than picking whichever level reads more cleanly. Most series here exist at both levels already (econ.state_wages next to econ.county_qcew; ag.pesticide_use_by_county carries state_fips for a free rollup; geo.counties joins the rest), so the second cut is usually one GROUP BY away.

SCOPE - do not fire this on everything. Step 3 applies to RELATIONSHIPS, not to counts or totals. 'How many people live in Texas' has no grain problem. A recipe that fires on every geographic question gets tuned out, which is how a real hazard becomes noise.

Related: pin-every-qualifier-before-summing-a-quickstats-shaped-table covers the different problem of ONE table whose rows mix units and geography levels internally (the fix there is constraining the query, not choosing a table). use-adjacent-cross-state-county-pairs-for-state-policy-effects is the specific design to reach for when a state policy admits a genuine bordering comparison.

recipes.title: A state-aid reduction (voucher deduction, formula cut) is not itself a net per-pupil loss until local revenue is checked for backfill
triggers: does state funding cut reduce spending
recipes.body:
A question asking how much public schools 'lose' per pupil when a state-aid stream is reduced (a voucher deduction, a formula change, an enrollment-driven cut) can be answered two different ways that are easy to conflate: the GROSS state-aid reduction itself, or the NET change in per-pupil spending after accounting for what districts do in response. These are not the same number, and reporting the gross figure as though it were the net effect overstates the harm whenever local revenue moves to offset it.

Measured directly in this harness (q15, school-vouchers-district-funding, 2026-09-03): an unaided expert-tier run surfaced a finding a warehouse-grounded run did not - Fordham Institute's academic study of Ohio's EdChoice program (Lavertu, OSU) found that even though EdChoice-affected districts' enrollment ran 10-15% lower than it otherwise would have, total per-pupil district SPENDING was statistically indistinguishable from what it would have been without the program, because local property-tax levies rose to backfill the state-aid reduction. A state-level diff-in-differences run against the exact same warehouse table used in that run (edu.f33_district_finance) never checked this - it correctly found no state-aggregate spending effect, but attributed that null to noise/insufficient power rather than testing the specific backfill mechanism the literature names.

edu.f33_district_finance already carries the columns needed to test this directly, in the same table a voucher-funding question would already be querying: state_revenue_thousand and local_revenue_thousand, both per-district per-year. Before reporting a state-aid decline (or a null state-aggregate spending effect) as the final word: compute the change in local_revenue_thousand per pupil over the same window for the same districts/states, and check whether it moved in the direction that would offset a state_revenue_thousand decline. A local-revenue rise that roughly tracks the state-revenue decline is evidence for the backfill mechanism; a local revenue that stayed flat or fell alongside state revenue is evidence the gap was NOT backfilled and the net loss claim stands. Report which case obtains, not just the gross state-aid figure - the two produce very different practical answers to 'how much do schools lose.'

recipes.title: A page/API returns blocked, 403, gzip-binary, or 'this table doesn't exist' — check whether a technique already worked elsewhere in THIS SAME session first
recipes.body:
The single most common way this connector's own comparative-eval scoring has cost a run first place, despite otherwise-equal work, is declaring a resource unreachable or a fact non-existent, when an access technique that would have solved it had ALREADY been used successfully earlier in the very same session for a different table or page. This is a retrieval-discipline gap, not a capability gap - the tool that would have worked was already in hand.

Measured directly across this harness's rejudge batch: one run used the Wayback Machine to route around a BLS 403 for one page, then later in the SAME answer declared BLS 'does not publish' a state-by-industry cross-tabulation without retrying that exact technique - a second persona reached the identical table by doing nothing more than what the first persona had already proven worked. Separately, a run declared no current state-level CO2/GDP series exists without checking whether EIA's own SEDS workbook (still actively updated) covered it, and another declared no consistent pre/post-2018 bridge-condition series existed without trying FHWA's own by-year publication pages directly.

Before writing 'X does not exist' / 'this table cannot be reached' / 'no such series is published': (1) check whether this SAME session already found a working access route for a DIFFERENT blocked resource (an archive-snapshot fetch, a mirror URL, a different file format, a state-level instead of federal endpoint) and try that exact route here before concluding the resource itself is the problem; (2) for a gzip-format static archive (a file literally named *.csv.gz, *.tar.gz, or one that returns as unparseable binary with Content-Type application/gzip or application/x-gzip), call web_fetch on it directly rather than treating the binary-content error as final - web_fetch auto-decompresses a raw gzip resource before content-type detection, so a NOAA/Census-style compressed archive that used to fail with 'unrecognized binary content type' now returns as plain text/CSV; (3) for a page or API that blocks on a naive bot-detection User-Agent string, web_fetch already presents an ordinary browser's header set, so a 403 that persists after that is more likely a real access wall (paywall, required auth) than a User-Agent problem, and should be reported as such rather than retried indefinitely.

The generalizable check, regardless of which specific technique applies: before a headline claim that something 'doesn't exist' or 'can't be reached,' name the SPECIFIC thing you tried and ask whether anything used successfully elsewhere this session applies here too. A resource being genuinely unavailable and a resource being unavailable to the specific approach tried so far are different findings, and only the first one licenses the strong claim.

recipes.title: Testing 'immigrants / ethnic enclaves / foreign-born areas have more crime' with warehouse data
recipes.body:
No arrest, offense or incarceration table in this corpus carries the offender's nativity, so 'immigrants commit crime at rate X' cannot be computed here directly; the published offender-rate studies (NIJ-funded Texas DPS arrest study, Light/He/Robey 2020 PNAS; Abramitzky et al. 2023 NBER w31440 incarceration by nativity 1870-2020) are the independent_value for that shape of claim.

The PLACE-level claim ('areas with more immigrants / ethnic enclaves have higher crime rates') IS testable here, at state grain, from two tables that join through geo.states:

  1. Foreign-born share: census.acs_nativity (population by nativity; use census.acs_nativity_by_education when only the 25+ population is needed) -> foreign_born / total by state and year. The `state` column is the 2-digit FIPS.
  2. Crime rate: crime.cde_offenses -> offense_rate (per 100k, one row per state x offense_code x month). Aggregate to state-year: AVG(offense_rate) or SUM over months, for offense_code 'violent-crime' and 'property-crime' separately. Join geo.states ON state_fips = acs.state to get state_abbr.
  3. Test: hypothesis_test (correlation) then ols_regression / robust_regression of crime_rate on foreign_born_share with at least poverty rate (census.acs_poverty) and urban share (geo.rural_urban_continuum or census population density) as controls; report the coefficient, its interval and p-value, and say plainly that it is cross-sectional and not causal.
  4. Chart: scatter of foreign-born share vs violent-crime rate by state, one point per state, with the fitted line.

A claim about enclaves is a claim about places; grade it on step 3, not on whether the speaker said it. The verdict for 'more immigrants -> more crime' is decided by the sign and significance of that coefficient; the published literature (Ousey & Kubrin 2018 meta-analysis; Adelman et al. 2017) is the comparison point, not the test.

recipes.title: Per-acre federal oil & gas royalty productivity, by state — and covering ALL leased states, not a sample
recipes.body:
A per-acre royalty-productivity question needs onrr_revenues (ONRR royalty revenue by state and fiscal year) joined to acreage by state and fiscal year. As of 2026-09-11 no leased-acreage or producing-acreage table exists in the lands schema -- but check LIVE with list_tables/search_catalog against lands each time rather than trusting this recipe text on that point, since this corpus is added to over time and the gap may have closed since this recipe was written. Only fall back to an external web_fetch against BLM's Public Land Statistics (blm.gov) for the acreage half of the join after that live check comes back empty.

Measured live (q46, 2026-09-11): a run that did this join correctly still lost on completeness because it published a table covering only 12 of the ~32 states with federal oil-and-gas leases, using only one denominator (producing acres), while a competing answer covered all 32 leased states with BOTH leased-acre and producing-acre denominators and a cross-state correlation statistic. The accuracy of the 12 states reported was fine -- the loss was scope, not correctness. There was no query row-limit forcing the stop; it was an unprompted self-truncation. This is the durable lesson regardless of where the acreage figures end up coming from.

Do not stop at a convenience sample of states. Enumerate every state onrr_revenues reports federal onshore royalty revenue for for the fiscal year(s) in scope, join every one of them to acreage, and report both leased-acre and producing-acre denominators side by side -- they answer different questions (how much of what's leased is actually producing being one of them) and a reader comparing states needs both, not just whichever was queried first.

recipes.title: A question asking whether one GROUP (places, or a demographic population) differs from another needs a matched/composition-adjusted comparison, not just a national aggregate ratio
recipes.body:
A national-level ratio between two groups (e.g. 'federal land burns 4x the rate of non-federal land', 'veterans have a 0.8-point lower unemployment rate than nonveterans') is easy to compute and easy to get wrong in a way that still produces a plausible-looking number: aggregating everything to one national total per group throws away a composition difference between the groups that can explain most or all of the raw gap on its own -- federal land is disproportionately concentrated in the arid West; veterans skew meaningfully older than nonveterans, and unemployment falls with age regardless of veteran status.

Measured live twice, same underlying shape: (q59, 2026-09-11) askamerica correctly joined a live ownership table, caught and disclosed a real defect in it, and cross-validated its national ratio against a second independent dataset -- genuinely good work -- but never left the national/annual grain, running no significance or confound test, where a comparison answer computed a WITHIN-STATE paired ratio for all 50 states and ran a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p=0.0004) plus a precipitation regression (r=-0.64) that explicitly tested and partially ruled out aridity/region as the real driver. (q78, 2026-09-12) askamerica fetched primary BLS data directly and added a genuine new disaggregation (disability status) neither baseline used, but never addressed the age-composition confound at all -- where a comparison answer cited an age-COMPOSITION-MATCHED comparison (veterans 3.24% vs. matched nonveterans 3.15%, showing the raw 0.7-0.9pp gap is largely an age-profile artifact) and pivoted to a metric that survives matching (labor-force participation, employment-to-population ratio) as the more honest headline.

FIX: when a question compares two groups -- places OR population subgroups -- don't stop at a national/pooled aggregate ratio even if it is well-sourced and cross-validated. For PLACES: join at the finer grain the comparison actually happens at (state, or county if the data supports it), compute the ratio or difference WITHIN each unit, and run a paired test across units (Wilcoxon signed-rank, or hypothesis_test/ols_regression for a continuous relationship). For POPULATION SUBGROUPS: check whether an obvious composition variable (age, sex, education) differs between the two groups and could explain the raw gap on its own -- age-standardize or find an already-matched comparison (e.g. NY Fed/BLS composition-matched series) rather than comparing raw group averages, and prefer a metric less sensitive to the confound (participation/employment-to-population rate over a raw unemployment-rate gap) as at least a secondary framing. Either way, if a plausible confound exists, test for it explicitly -- a correlation, regression, or matched comparison against the confounding variable, stated plainly as a confound check, not folded silently into the main analysis.

recipes.title: A majority-literature synthesis on a contested empirical claim should name a known, specific dissenting critique, not just present the consensus view as unanimous
recipes.body:
A question with a clear majority position in the published literature is easy to answer by synthesizing the supporting studies and stopping there, because they already agree with each other and read as settled. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is treating majority agreement as unanimity -- many contested empirical topics also have a specific, named dissenting critique (a different research group disputing the data, the methodology, or the measurement), and a synthesis that never mentions it presents the topic as more settled than it actually is, even when the majority conclusion is correct.

Measured directly in this harness (q241, 2026-09-21): asked whether immigrants commit more or less crime than natives, an askamerica run correctly synthesized the majority literature (Texas DPS/Light-He-Robey PNAS 2020, Cato Institute incarceration data, Abramitzky et al.'s 150-year historical study) and additionally ran an original OLS regression against the warehouse confirming no state-level relationship between foreign-born share and crime rate -- genuinely strong work. But it never mentioned the Center for Immigration Studies' published critique disputing the Texas DPS data's undercount of illegal-immigrant offenders, even though it drew on the same Cato source material. Two independently-run unaided personas (no connector, web research only) both found and disclosed the CIS dispute on their own -- the strongest possible signal that this is a real, reachable gap, not a hypothetical one.

FIX: when researching a contested empirical claim, run a second, explicit search pass for the dissenting side -- terms like "[topic] critique", "[topic] disputes", "[topic] methodology controversy", "[claim] debunked" alongside the supporting-evidence search -- rather than stopping once enough literature supports one conclusion. Name the dissenting group and the substance of its argument in the answer even when the majority conclusion still stands after weighing it; a reader should learn the topic has a real live dispute, not just its winning side.

recipes.title: A self-computed real-dollar (inflation-adjusted) figure that disagrees with an independently-cited real series is not automatically the wrong one -- reconcile the two, don't silently pick one
recipes.body:
adjust_inflation deflates a nominal dollar figure against one CPI series to a chosen base year. A well-known metric like real median household income also has independently published "real" series (Census's own historical table; FRED's MEHOINUSA672N), and it is tempting to treat a gap between your own adjust_inflation result and one of these published series as proof your own number is wrong. It usually is not -- multiple real-dollar series for the SAME nominal figures routinely diverge for two ordinary, legitimate reasons: (1) different price INDEX methodology (headline CPI-U vs. the chain-weighted C-CPI-U / R-CPI-U-RS blend FRED uses, which are built differently and produce different cumulative multi-decade inflation estimates), and (2) different BASE YEAR (FRED's series re-expresses its whole history in the CURRENT release year's dollars each update, e.g. "2024 dollars" for a 2023 data point, rather than the survey year's own dollars the way Census's own report states it -- so the same year's income can appear as two different-looking numbers depending on which convention was used).

Measured directly in this harness (q242, 2026-09-21): fact-checking a claim that household income "more than doubled since 2000", an askamerica run computed real growth as ~8.5% via adjust_inflation, while two unaided personas separately cited FRED's MEHOINUSA672N and reported ~15% and ~19%. On inspection, FRED's own 2000 value ($73,560, in FRED's 2024-dollar terms) is within 1% of askamerica's own computed 2000 figure ($74,300, in 2023-dollar terms) -- the two approaches actually agree closely on the STARTING point. The apparent gap traces almost entirely to the 2023 ENDPOINT: FRED's $84,730 is expressed in 2024 dollars (one more year of inflation baked in on both sides of FRED's own ratio), while Census's own P60-282 states the actual 2023 figure, in 2023 dollars, as $80,610. Neither figure is fabricated or simply wrong; they answer the question in two different, both-legitimate units. The lesson is not "prefer the published series" -- it is that nobody in that run noticed or explained the divergence.

FIX: when a self-computed real-dollar figure and an independently-cited real series disagree by more than a rounding difference, do not silently report one and drop the other. Check whether they used the same base year and the same price index; if either differs, say so explicitly and either recompute both sides onto one common index/base year before comparing, or report the range across methodologies rather than a single point figure presented as settled. A reconciled range or a named methodology difference is more honest, and often more useful to the reader, than confidently picking whichever number came from the 'official-sounding' source.

recipes.title: When a topic's key figures come from a compiled secondary aggregator and the corpus has no purpose-built table for it, search separately for the major primary study the aggregator is built on
recipes.body:
A well-compiled secondary aggregator (Our World in Data, a think-tank fact sheet, a Wikipedia summary table) is an efficient way to get a topic's headline comparison figures in one place, and it is tempting to stop there once its numbers answer the question. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is treating the aggregator as sufficient sourcing on its own -- a major, independently-run primary study often exists behind or alongside it, using an entirely different dataset and methodology, and citing it both strengthens the answer's evidentiary base and surfaces nuance (sample period, population covered, what exactly was measured) the aggregator's summary table flattens away.

Measured directly in this harness (q12, 2026-09-22): asked which power source is most dangerous per unit of electricity, an askamerica run correctly cited Our World in Data's compiled deaths-per-TWh figures (built on Markandya & Wilkinson 2007) and reached the right ranking (coal > gas > nuclear), but never searched for or found Henneman et al., *Science* (2023) -- a Medicare-linked mortality study covering 480 US coal plants, 1999-2020, attributing ~460,000 deaths to coal-plant PM2.5 from an entirely different dataset and methodology than the 2007 European baseline. Two independently-run unaided personas both found and cited this study on their own -- the strongest possible signal this is a real, reachable gap. The energy/health schemas in this corpus have no purpose-built energy-source mortality table at all, so this was never a case of missing a corpus query -- it was an external-literature search that stopped one source short.

FIX: when the corpus has no table for a topic and the answer is built from a compiled secondary source, run a second, explicit search pass for the primary study/studies the compilation rests on or that independently corroborate the same figures from different data -- terms like "[topic] study", "[topic] peer-reviewed", "[aggregator]'s own source for [figure]" -- before finalizing the answer. A second independent primary source that agrees with the aggregator is stronger evidence than the aggregator alone, and if it disagrees, that disagreement is itself worth surfacing rather than missing entirely.

recipes.title: "How concentrated is X" for a market with a distinct infrastructure/access structure is not answered by concentration at only one layer
triggers: down to a handful of firms
recipes.body:
Many markets a caller asks to size the concentration of are not one flat market but two stacked layers: an infrastructure/utility layer (an exchange, a clearinghouse, a platform) and an access/intermediary layer (the brokers, banks, or sellers who actually reach end customers through it). It is tempting to treat the question as answered once the layer the corpus's own data can reach is fully worked out, especially when that layer turns out to be extremely concentrated on its own -- but a reader asking "is this down to a handful of firms" usually means the whole business, and the access layer is often AT LEAST as concentrated as the infrastructure layer, sometimes more.

Measured directly in this harness (q38, 2026-09-22): asked how concentrated interest-rate swap clearing is, an askamerica run correctly identified that its own CFTC swap-data tables cannot see the CCP (clearinghouse) side at all -- a real, permanent data-source limitation (Part 43 public dissemination excludes the CCP-facing novation leg by design) -- and built an excellent CCP-layer analysis from external sources instead (HHI=8,250, LCH SwapClear ~91% of global cleared notional). But it never addressed the SEPARATE dealer/clearing-member layer -- which banks control client access to that clearing -- even though nothing about the CFTC-table limitation blocks researching that layer. Two independently-run unaided personas both found and reported it on their own (OCC data: 4 US banks hold 87.1% of bank derivatives notional; a Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago study: 5 bank-affiliated clearing members hold over 80% of client margin for cleared IRS), which is at least as concentrated a picture as the CCP layer and materially changes what "a handful of firms" means for this market.

FIX: before finalizing an answer to a market-concentration question, name the distinct layers the market actually has (infrastructure/utility vs. access/intermediary is the most common split, but a market can have others -- upstream supplier concentration vs. downstream retail concentration, for example) and check whether each one is addressed, not just the layer the corpus happens to have data for. A data limitation on ONE layer is never a reason the other layer went unresearched -- that second layer is usually reachable through ordinary external search even when the corpus has nothing on it.

recipes.title: Before attributing a cross-sectional relationship to a proposed cause, test whether the outcome predicts the cause going the other direction
triggers: which way does the relationship run
does X cause Y or Y cause X
recipes.body:
A question phrased as 'did states that did X see better outcomes' invites running a cross-sectional regression of the later outcome on the earlier proposed cause and reading a significant coefficient as support for the causal story implied by the question's own wording. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is stopping there: a real coefficient in the hypothesized direction is consistent with the causal story, but it is equally consistent with the reverse -- richer places having more resources to spend on the 'cause' in the first place, not the 'cause' having produced the outcome.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question asking whether investing in education/infrastructure or keeping taxes low produced better income growth since 2010, the highest-scoring run ran an explicit reverse regression -- regressing 2010 income level on SUBSEQUENT per-pupil education spending -- and found states richer in 2010 went on to spend MORE per pupil (r=0.59), a real threat to any 'spending caused growth' reading that a same-direction-only analysis would never surface. A second run reached the same core forward finding (no tax-burden/income relationship) but never ran this check and so could not rule out the same confound.

FIX: whenever a question's own phrasing implies a direction of causation between two time-ordered or plausibly-endogenous variables, run the regression in BOTH directions before reporting either coefficient as evidence of the implied direction -- regress the later outcome on the earlier proposed cause, AND regress the earlier proposed-cause's own starting level on the outcome (or on the proposed cause's subsequent change) to check whether the outcome's initial condition predicts the 'cause' just as well or better. Report both coefficients together; a forward relationship that survives being checked in reverse is far stronger evidence than one that was only ever tested in the direction the question suggested. This is a distinct check from a VIF/collinearity check between two competing predictors (see correlated-predictors-need-a-vif-check) -- collinearity asks whether two candidate causes are proxies for each other; this asks whether the proposed cause is itself downstream of the outcome.

recipes.title: A real correlation, regression, or concentration finding is a description, not an explanation - test what actually drives it when the corpus has the ingredients
recipes.body:
Reporting a real, correctly-computed quantitative finding - a correlation, a fixed-effects regression, a state dominating a total - is easy to treat as the finished answer, because it IS a genuine result and stopping there is not wrong, only incomplete. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is describing the pattern (which state dominates, how tightly two series correlate, that a regional split exists) without taking the one further step available in the same corpus to explain WHY - and a described-but-unexplained pattern is a materially thinner answer than one that names its driver.

Measured directly in this harness, three separate instances: (1) a question about whether tax cuts or education spending grew incomes found both null, and separately found the two predictors were themselves collinear (r=0.98) - but never tested whether an EARLIER value of the outcome predicted the LATER value of the proposed cause, the standard reverse-causality check a real relationship would need (moot here since both relationships were null, but the gap is the missing check, not this run's stakes); (2) a question about which state dominates federal oil/gas royalty revenue correctly found and quantified the dominant state's share, but never tested whether leased ACREAGE SIZE correlates with revenue at all - the run that did found acreage barely predicts revenue (r=0.54, rising to r=0.85 excluding the dominant state), meaning formation QUALITY, not quantity, drives the concentration - a materially different and more useful finding than the raw share alone; (3) a question about whether crop-insurance payouts track drought found a real two-way fixed-effects panel result AND a striking regional split (Plains states tracking tightly, Southeast states inverted) but explicitly declined to test any candidate mechanism for the split, leaving it as 'the likely mechanism, not separately regression-tested here' - when the same corpus's policy-type/coverage-plan columns could have tested the leading candidate directly.

FIX: after reporting a correlation, regression, or concentration/skew finding, ask whether the corpus holds a further, reachable test of WHY it holds - a scale/size variable to correlate against the outcome (does quantity explain the skew, or does something else?), a reverse-direction or lagged version of the same regression (does the outcome predict the cause, undermining the causal story?), or a categorical column that could test a named candidate mechanism (a policy type, a coverage plan, a formation type) directly rather than leaving it as an unverified aside. Not every question has a reachable next step - but before treating a described pattern as the finished answer, check for one.

recipes.title: A single old external study's headline figure should be recomputed from current corpus data when the corpus holds (or can be joined to reach) both halves of the calculation
recipes.body:
A 'does the payment cover the cost' or 'does X compensate for Y' question is easy to answer by finding the one study that already computed a comparable ratio and reporting its headline figure, because it looks authoritative and directly on-point. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is treating that figure as current when it is not, without checking whether the corpus - possibly by joining two different schemas, not just querying one table - already holds the ingredients to recompute it for the present day.

Measured directly in this harness: asked whether federal PILT payments to counties cover the property tax counties can't collect on federal land, one run found the ONLY national tax-equivalency study in existence - a real, well-sourced 1999 USDA Forest Service report using FY1997 data - and reported its implied ~30% coverage ratio as the answer, without attempting a current recomputation despite having the payment-side table (`lands.pilt_county_payments`) already queried and a Census county government-finance table (property-tax revenue by county) plausibly reachable in the same corpus's fiscal schema - confirmed reachable because a DIFFERENT run in the same session used exactly that fiscal table for an unrelated question. Two independently-run unaided personas, using two different methods (an original current dataset build, and independent case-study literature), both converged on a materially lower current coverage ratio (1.5%-11%, not ~30%) - meaning the 26-year-old study was not just old but likely wrong by a factor of 3-6x for today.

FIX: when the best available quantified answer to a compensation/coverage/shortfall question is a single study more than a few years old, and the corpus holds one side of the underlying calculation already, check for the OTHER side before reporting the stale figure as the headline number - including checking a different schema than the one the first half came from; the two halves of a 'does the payment cover the cost' question often live in different domains (a payments table in one schema, a tax/finance table in another) and are easy to treat as unconnected because they were never queried in the same session. A current, corpus-built recomputation is a stronger answer than even a well-sourced old study, and the old study still has value - as context for how the ratio has moved over time, not as the headline number itself.

recipes.title: A headline mortality or risk figure built from a dose-response model or an old epidemiological baseline needs its assumption and vintage disclosed, not just the number
recipes.body:
A cross-technology or cross-source mortality/risk comparison (e.g. nuclear vs. coal vs. gas deaths per unit of power) is easy to answer by citing the standard published per-TWh figures and stopping there, because they already look precise and are widely repeated. The plausible-but-wrong shortcut is treating a modeled estimate as equivalent in kind to a confirmed count, and treating an old epidemiological baseline as still current, without saying either thing to the reader.

Measured directly in this harness: on a question ranking nuclear/coal/gas by health risk, the highest-scoring run explicitly disclosed two things a lower-scoring run did not: (1) nuclear's low headline death toll rests on a linear-no-threshold (LNT) dose-response model that is itself contested -- only 46 deaths are directly confirmed (Chernobyl/Fukushima combined), against a MODELED range of 4,000-60,000+ from the same events depending on the LNT assumption -- and (2) the standard fossil-fuel mortality figures trace to a 2007 European study, and more recent PM2.5 epidemiology suggests that baseline likely UNDERSTATES current risk by 4-9x, meaning the standard comparison is not just old but probably biased in a specific, statable direction.

FIX: when reporting a mortality/risk figure, check and disclose two things before treating it as settled: (a) whether the figure is a directly confirmed count or the output of a dose-response/extrapolation model, and if the latter, name the model's key contested assumption and the range it produces under that assumption, not just the point estimate; (b) the publication year of the underlying epidemiological baseline, and whether more recent research in the same field has revised the exposure-response relationship it depends on -- a quick check of whether newer studies exist and which direction they'd move the estimate is enough; a full re-derivation is not required, but silence on a known, checkable staleness is.

recipes.title: SUM() through a LEFT JOIN wrapped in COALESCE(...,0) or CAST(...) throws a planner type-mismatch error
recipes.body:
Writing COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) (or CAST(COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) AS ...)) where x comes from the nullable side of a LEFT JOIN, combined with GROUP BY on two or more columns (or any other aggregate alongside it, e.g. COUNT(*)), triggers a genuine Apache Calcite core planner bug: an IllegalArgumentException 'Type mismatch: ... VARCHAR -> DOUBLE NOT NULL' (or similar) thrown from ProjectMergeRule/EnumerableProjectToCalcRule during planning, before any data is read. This is not a data or schema problem -- the underlying column really is the declared numeric type in production.

Root cause (traced 2026-09-26, ops#439): SUM is reduced by default (AggregateReduceFunctionsRule) into CASE WHEN COUNT(x) = 0 THEN NULL ELSE SUM0(x) END whenever the argument is nullable. That reduction shares a Map<AggregateCall, RexNode> cache across every aggregate call in the same Aggregate node, and AggregateCall.equals()/hashCode() intentionally ignore the call's return type -- so an internal null-check COUNT call generated by this reduction can collide with an unrelated, differently-typed aggregate call already in the cache and hand back a stale RexNode. Wrapping the aggregate in a subquery does not help; the planner inlines it back before the bug fires. This needs a real Calcite core fix (rule-by-rule trace + regression test in core/), which is a separate, larger piece of work from a single query.

FIX: rewrite the query to use an explicit CASE instead of COALESCE around the SUM -- semantically identical, does not trigger the bug: CASE WHEN SUM(x) IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE SUM(x) END. Apply any outer CAST to that CASE expression exactly as you would have applied it to the COALESCE. Confirmed correct against the same repro that fails with COALESCE.

recipes.title: A weighted aggregate across a small-n group of unequal-sized units owes a with/without-the-biggest-unit check
triggers: aggregate percentage across a small group
does one county drive the number
recipes.body:
Computing a single pooled/weighted percentage or rate across a small set of geographic units (a few dozen counties, states, or facilities) risks reporting a number that describes one dominant unit rather than the group -- and unlike an explicit exclusion, there is no WHERE clause or diagnostic to flag it, because every unit really is included.

Measured directly in this harness (q127, 2026-09-27, comparative-eval rerun): asked what share of housing in high-seismic-risk counties predates modern building codes, one run reported a single pooled figure (58.1% across 48 counties) with no further breakdown. A second, independently-run analysis on the same underlying question computed the same kind of pooled aggregate (53.8% across 40 counties) but went further: it also reported the UNWEIGHTED median across counties (49.9% -- essentially at the national baseline), and recomputed the aggregate with the single largest county removed (53.8% -> 49.4%, a 4.4-point swing from one unit out of 40). That second run's version made it clear the pooled figure was being pulled up mainly by one or two very large, very old urban counties, not reflecting a 'typical' high-risk county -- a materially more complete and more defensible answer to the same question, using data both runs already had.

FIX: whenever you report one pooled/weighted number across a group of fewer than roughly 100 geographic or entity units, do two cheap extra things before finishing: (1) compute the UNWEIGHTED average/median across the same units and report it alongside the weighted figure -- a large gap between the two means the weighted number describes a handful of big units, not the group; (2) identify the single largest unit by whatever you are weighting on (population, housing units, dollars) and recompute the aggregate with it excluded, reporting the delta. If the two figures agree closely, say so -- that itself strengthens the pooled number. If they diverge, the divergence is part of the answer, not a footnote to omit. This is the same discipline as report-what-an-exclusion-changed-not-only-that-you-made-one, applied proactively to an aggregate you have NOT excluded anything from, rather than reactively to one you have.

recipes.title: When a question asks 'how concentrated/what share', and you already queried the raw counts to compute it, do the arithmetic yourself rather than citing an older external report's headline percentage
triggers: percent of total accounted for by
cite the GAO figure instead of computing
recipes.body:
A 'how concentrated is X in Y' question asks for a share: (claims/dollars/units attributable to the concentrated group) / (claims/dollars/units overall). When both halves of that fraction are already sitting in front of you from live queries you already ran, the correct answer is to divide them yourself -- not to reach for an older published report's percentage as the headline figure, even when that report is a good, citable, authoritative source.

Measured directly in this harness (q124, 2026-09-27, comparative-eval rerun): asked how concentrated NFIP flood claims are in repeat-loss properties, one run queried a live property-level file, correctly extracted and reported the full per-property claim-count distribution (123,737 properties with exactly 2 claims, 57,305 with 3, 27,319 with 4, ~28,565 with 5-9, 3,049 with 10+) AND separately queried the total claims count from a second live table (2,755,527) -- everything needed to compute a current claims-share was already in hand. Instead of summing the distribution and dividing, the run's headline answer was FEMA/GAO's own already-published figure (48% of claim DOLLARS, as of December 2021), a different basis (dollars, not counts) and a different vintage (2021, not the 2026 snapshot just queried. A second, independently-run analysis on the same question did the arithmetic: summed the same kind of per-property distribution (740,000 total claims from repeat-loss properties) against the live total (2,721,780), computing 27.2% -- a current, count-basis, self-verified figure -- and separately, explicitly, cited the older GAO/Pew dollar-basis figures as historical cross-checks rather than as the answer itself.

FIX: before finishing a 'how concentrated / what share' answer, check whether you already queried both the numerator (the concentrated group's count/dollar total) and the denominator (the overall total) in this session. If you did, compute the share yourself and lead with that self-computed, current, basis-matched figure -- then cite any external report's percentage as a cross-check/sanity-check alongside it (do the two agree? what basis or vintage difference explains a gap, per compute-real-dollar-figure-against-independently-cited-series' reconciliation discipline), never as a substitute for arithmetic you already had the inputs to do. An externally-cited percentage is a good SECOND check, not a first-choice ANSWER, whenever the raw counts to compute your own are already on the table.

recipes.title: When neither variable of a hypothesized correlation exists at the grain asked for, the finding of absence is not the whole answer — still enumerate the confounds that would have to be controlled if the data did exist
triggers: does X actually cause more Y at the county level
correlation cannot be tested at this grain
data doesn't exist at county grain
neither variable is published at that level
recipes.body:
A question asking whether some county/local-level condition (older infrastructure, weaker institutions, lower quality systems) correlates with an outcome sometimes turns out to be untestable because neither the independent nor the dependent variable is published at that grain -- claims data proprietary below state level, a quality/age index that was never compiled, etc. Confirming that absence, and reporting the best available coarser-grain evidence, is real and valuable work. But stopping at 'the mechanism is plausible but unverified' leaves out something a rigorous analyst would still do even with no data in hand: name the specific confounds that would have to be controlled before a raw correlation (if the data existed) could be read as anything more than coincidence.

Measured directly in this harness (q183, 2026-09-28, comparative-eval fresh run): asked whether counties with older/lower-quality property-recording systems generate more title-insurance claims, one run correctly established that no public source publishes county-level claims or a county-level recording-quality index, cited the best available national cause-of-claims breakdown, and closed with 'treat any strong claim of a county-level correlation as an untested hypothesis.' A second, independently-run analysis reached the identical data-absence finding and cited much of the same evidence, but added an explicit confounding-and-causal-caveats section naming the specific variables (property age, transaction volume, urban/rural mix, title-plant coverage, local fraud exposure) that move together with county age/development independent of the recording system itself, and named the design (county/policy-level fixed effects, or a before/after comparison around a specific county's e-recording go-live date) that would be needed to isolate the effect even if the data appeared. That second answer is more useful to a reader who might later find county-level data somewhere this search didn't reach -- it tells them what to control for, not just that nobody has tested it.

FIX: whenever a question's premise turns out to be untestable at the requested grain, don't stop at reporting the absence and calling the mechanism 'plausible but unverified.' Spend one more paragraph naming the two or three most obvious confounds a raw correlation would carry if the data did exist (what else moves with the proposed cause and could independently drive the proposed effect), and name the study design that would isolate it. This turns a dead end into a usable roadmap for the next person who tries the question, and is cheap to do since it requires no additional data -- only the same causal-inference reasoning already applied to whatever coarser-grain evidence was found.

recipes.title: 'Lost the last X' (branch, store, hospital, school) means went from ANY positive count to zero -- not only from exactly one to zero
recipes.body:
'How many X lost their last Y' asks for every X that went from Y > 0 to Y = 0 over the window -- it does not restrict to X that started at exactly Y = 1. An entity that had two branches and closed both has just as certainly 'lost its last branch' as one that had exactly one and closed it; excluding the two-or-more-to-zero cases produces a real undercount of the thing the question is actually asking about, not a stricter or more careful version of the same answer.

Measured directly in this harness (q168, 2026-09-28, comparative-eval fresh run): asked how many rural counties lost their last remaining bank branch over ten years, one run queried the connector's branch-deposits table with a starting condition of exactly 1 branch dropping to 0, explicitly self-flagging it as 'a deliberately narrow definition that is a lower bound.' A second, independently-run analysis against the same underlying FDIC branch-level data used the natural reading (>= 1 branch in the start year, 0 in the end year) and found three additional counties the narrower query structurally could not find -- each had had two branches, both of which closed. Only 4 of the two runs' 7 named counties overlapped; the exactly-1-vs->=1 starting condition, not a data quality difference, was the larger cause (both runs used the correct branch-level, not headquarters-level, county field).

FIX: for any 'lost the last X' / 'dropped to zero' / 'no longer has any Y' question, filter on the END state being zero and the START state being any positive count (> 0), never restrict the START state to exactly 1. If a narrower definition is used for a specific reason (e.g. isolating single-branch-to-zero closures as a distinct sub-case), report the >=1-to-zero figure as the headline answer to the question as actually asked, and the narrower cut as a secondary breakdown -- not the reverse. This generalizes to any 'lost its last remaining' framing: bank branches, hospitals, grocery stores, schools, pharmacies -- the same >=1-to-zero filter is the correct operationalization regardless of domain.

recipes.title: Prediction markets: price an event against a catalog forecast, then build baskets — both venues, net of fees
recipes.body:
Prediction-market questions ('find a mispriced event', 'find 5 events mispriced by more than 10%', 'find a basket that locks in a yield over 10%') run through the market tools, and every one of them reads BOTH Kalshi and Polymarket.

MISPRICING (one event). 1) find_market_candidates (sample=N for a random draw) lists events that settle on a quantity this catalog holds, with the govdata_tables and the forecasting tool that fits (forecast_with). 2) price_market_event(source, event_id) with no forecast returns the rules: read the exact series, period, units, rounding and release date. 3) Forecast that settlement value: price_market_event(source, event_id, build_forecast=true) builds the forecast from the settlement series inside the engine and returns forecast_built with its series, transform, last_period and flags; state every flag. When build_forecast fails because the builder does not resolve the event's series, forecast it from the catalog: a federal release -> arima_forecast on the settlement series, passing forecast and forecast_std_error at the settlement period as mean + sd (or mean + lower + upper + level); a weather reading -> samples_sql of the same station and calendar window in every past year; a traded price -> volatility_forecast, passing price_band.price_median + cumulative_vol_pct (check the vol model with backtest_volatility; a band, not a direction); a regression forecast (ols_regression, flexible_regression) -> cross_validate it first, then mean + sd. Check data_coverage: a table that stops before the settlement period is forecasting further ahead than it looks. 4) price_market_event with the forecast: edge = fair - price - fee, in probability points. 'Mispriced by more than 10%' and 'mispriced with a spread of more than 10%' both mean edge >= 0.10 (min_edge=0.10) unless return on cost is asked for; say which. The spread in a mispricing question is the gap between fair value and price, not the bid-ask spread: do not screen events on median_spread. 5) Price each other_venue counterpart with the same forecast. A forecast median far from implied_median is more often a misread rule or stale data than an edge: recheck before reporting.

A RANDOM MISPRICED EVENT, OR N OF THEM. 'Find a mispriced event' is N = 1. You MUST call scan_market_opportunities first (min_edge as asked, limit >= N; call again while status is loading or scanning). It forecasts and prices every candidate event inside the engine and returns the ones past min_edge, with funnel counts and the reasons the rest were not forecast. Pick at random among its opportunities and vet at most 3 with price_market_event(source, event_id, build_forecast=true): confirm the forecast's series, period and rounding are what the rules name, and state every flag, confidence and baseline_vs_market. The scan's forecast is a baseline any participant can compute; market_inside_baseline_range means the market is only more certain than the baseline, which is weak evidence against a heavily traded market. Report funnel: how many events were matched, forecast and passed. When fewer than N pass, say so. Draw with find_market_candidates(sample) only for an event the scan could not forecast, and never fill the list with events that were not forecast.

CONFIDENCE. An edge from the engine's forecast is only as good as that forecast's record against the venue's price. backtest_market_forecast(source='kalshi', series) rebuilds the forecast as of days_before days before each past settled event of the series and scores it and the venue's price at that moment against the outcome (Brier score, hit rate): baseline_beats_market, market_beats_baseline or inconclusive. price_market_event and the scan carry confidence: backtested (the engine built the forecast, no blocking flag, the baseline beat the price) or weak, with reasons. For a Kalshi edge whose confidence.backtest is null you MUST run the backtest and state its verdict, events scored and revision caveat. A series where the price beat the baseline is left out of the scan; a disagreement there is the baseline being wrong. Polymarket events have no backtest: say so.

ACTING ON IT. Quotes are a point in time and nothing is traded for the user. Each mispriced market carries a ticket: side, limit_price (the most to pay and still clear min_edge after the fee), depth (contracts and dollars resting at or under that limit; pass size to get the fill price for that many contracts), quote_time and void_conditions (the market's close; the next release of the settlement series). Report limit_price, depth and void_conditions with each opportunity, plus annualized_return_simple_365d and breakeven_fair (the fair value at which the edge is zero). Asked later whether it is still there, you MUST call requote_market_opportunity(ticket): open, partly_open (contracts_left), gone, or void when a void condition has occurred. A re-quote reads the book again and does not recompute the fair value.

ARBITRAGE (a basket). A basket is a set of correlated events bought at prices that improve the odds of a positive outcome; a lock is a basket whose worst case still pays more than it cost after fees. find_market_baskets proposes them. cross_venue first: the same quantity quoted on Kalshi and on Polymarket, closing within days, needs no forecast -> price_market_basket(events=[both, same column, Polymarket conditions in that column's units], lock=true, scenario_grid=true, search=2..4, min_yield as asked). Read both rules texts: two events are one outcome only if source, period and rounding agree. Other recipes (same_place, linked_drivers such as weather + crop yield + commodity prices + tariffs + inflation, series_run): measure the link with fetch_aligned_series and correlation_matrix, forecast each event, then price_market_basket with joint scenarios — scenarios_sql over the aligned history keeps the correlation; scenario_sweep rows work inline.

FEES. Every edge, floor and yield is net of a taker fee at the quote: Kalshi 0.07 x fee_multiplier x p x (1-p) per contract, Polymarket its per-market fee schedule (zero where fees are off). Fees are largest at 50 cents and are paid on every leg, so a basket's gross gap of a few points is routinely gone after fees — report the gross gap and the net result. Position limits and cost of capital are not modelled. For one event, depth is read for the 3 largest edges and annualized_return_simple_365d is simple, not compounded; a basket's yield is to settlement, not annualized, and its depth is not read.

REPORT, per event: venue, forecast source table and its last period, fair, price, fee, edge, confidence and backtest verdict, limit_price, depth, void_conditions, volume or open interest, days to close, what would make the forecast wrong. Per basket: legs with venue and side, cost, fees, floor, yield, the scenario basis and row count. 'No mispricing above the threshold' and 'no lock after fees' are findings: report them with the closest case. DETAIL RECIPES (find_recipe): forecasting by driver, 'prediction-market-forecast-cpi-pce-food-prices', 'prediction-market-forecast-jobs-unemployment-claims', 'prediction-market-forecast-gdp-and-output', 'prediction-market-forecast-mortgage-rate-and-housing', 'prediction-market-forecast-weather-and-climatology', 'prediction-market-forecast-oil-price-barrier'; basket structures, 'prediction-market-basket-cross-venue', 'prediction-market-basket-same-place', 'prediction-market-basket-linked-drivers', 'prediction-market-basket-series-run', 'prediction-market-basket-range', 'prediction-market-basket-calendar'; acting on an opportunity, 'prediction-market-capture-a-point-in-time-opportunity'.

recipes.title: Forecasting a CPI, PCE or food-price event on Kalshi or Polymarket: forecast_market_event picks the series from the rules, and every flag is stated
recipes.body:
Drivers inflation (title matches cpi or inflation), pce and food_prices are resolved by the forecast builder. Build the forecast with price_market_event(source, event_id, build_forecast=true), or forecast_market_event(source, event_id) to read the forecast alone. Do it for the event on each venue, Kalshi and Polymarket, that settles on the same release.

SERIES. The builder reads the title and rules. All items: CPIAUCSL (seasonally adjusted, econ.fred_indicators) or CUUR0000SA0 (not adjusted, econ.inflation_metrics). Core ('core', 'less food and energy'): CPILFESL or CUUR0000SA0L1E. Where the rules state the adjustment it decides; where they are silent a year-over-year event takes the not-adjusted series and any other transform the adjusted one. A series id the rules name is used as named (CUSR0000SA0 resolves to CPIAUCSL, CUSR0000SA0L1E to CPILFESL); an id the catalog does not carry returns series_not_sourced and no forecast. PCE: PCEPI, or PCEPILFE when the text says core. Food: CUUR0000SAF11 for 'food at home' or 'grocery', CUUR0000SEFV for 'food away'; an egg-price event names APU0000708111, which the builder returns as series_not_sourced (BLS average-price series, govdata-ops issue 851). A CPI component (shelter, rent, food, energy, gasoline, apparel, used cars, medical, airfares, electricity, new vehicles) is not resolved: the call fails and says to pass series and table, or series_sql.

TRANSFORM. mom_pct or yoy_pct is read from the title, then the rules; both present is an error and transform must be passed. An index event worded 'increases by more than X%' with no 12-month wording is read as mom_pct. A CPI series has no default transform: when the text says neither, the call fails and asks for transform.

METHOD. The distribution is empirical: past changes of the same transform applied to the latest level. yoy_pct: the latest year-over-year percent plus each historical h-period change in the year-over-year percent, h being the months from last_period to settlement_period; it needs the value 12 months before settlement, so a settlement more than 12 periods past the last row fails. mom_pct: historical one-month percent changes, and for a series not known to be seasonally adjusted only changes of the settlement's calendar month. Default history is 15 years of monthly rows (years overrides); fewer than 8 samples is an error. A settlement month the catalog already holds is an error: query the value. With as_of, a monthly row counts only once its release has printed: CPI 16 days after month end, PCE 31.

FLAGS. You MUST state every flag. seasonal_adjustment_mismatch: the rules and the series differ on adjustment. rounding_unverified: the rules state no rounding, so values are compared with strikes unrounded; rounding_mismatch: round passed differs from the rules. units_mismatch: the rules' units are not the series'. last_period_before_settlement: more than one month lies between the catalog's last row and settlement, and the forecast bridges them. history_stale: the latest row is more than 45 days past its following month's end. history_gap: months with no value. seasonal_adjustment_mismatch, units_mismatch, rounding_mismatch and history_stale are the flags scan_market_opportunities treats as blocking.

WHEN NOT TO TRUST IT. A blocking flag; series_not_sourced (you MUST NOT price against a forecast of another series); a median far from the market's implied_median, which is more often a misread rule than an edge. The forecast knows nothing the series does not: no nowcast, no news. A Kalshi edge also needs backtest_market_forecast(source='kalshi', series=<venue series, e.g. KXCPI or KXCPIYOY>) when confidence.backtest is null. Polymarket has no backtest: say so.

recipes.title: Forecasting a payrolls, unemployment or jobless-claims event on Kalshi or Polymarket: which series, which units, and what the sample is
recipes.body:
Drivers payrolls (title matches payrolls, jobs added, nonfarm, jobs report, jobs numbers), unemployment (unemployment, u-3) and jobless_claims (jobless claims, initial claims) are resolved by the forecast builder. Build with price_market_event(source, event_id, build_forecast=true) or forecast_market_event(source, event_id), for the event on each venue.

PAYROLLS. CES0000000001 total nonfarm, or CES0500000001 when the text says private; both seasonally adjusted, monthly, in thousands (econ.employment_statistics). Default transform is change: the sample is every one-month change in the level over the history window (years, default 15), not applied to the latest level. A window that contains an outlier month carries it in the sample; years shortens the window. Units: when the title and rules state no units and say 'jobs', the samples and last_value are multiplied by 1000 so they are in jobs, the unit a venue strikes in; when they state no units and do not say 'jobs', units_mismatch is flagged and the forecast is unverified against the strikes; rules that state a unit the series is not in (for example millions) also flag units_mismatch. Pass samples in the strikes' units when it is flagged.

UNEMPLOYMENT. LNS14000000 (U-3 headline, seasonally adjusted), or LNS13327709 (U-6) when the text says u-6. A demographic rate (black, hispanic, latino, asian, white, women, men, teen, veterans, youth) is not resolved: the call fails and asks for series and table. Default transform is level, additive: historical h-period changes in percentage points added to the latest rate, h being the months to settlement_period. The builder reads the rounding from the title and rules; where neither states one the flag rounding_unverified is returned. round is rejected with build_forecast=true.

JOBLESS CLAIMS. ICSA initial, or CCSA when the text says continuing; weekly, seasonally adjusted, persons, level, proportional changes (econ.fred_indicators). The settlement date is the event's close date unless settlement_period is given; h = ceil(days from the last row / 7). history_stale applies past 7 days.

RELEASE TIMING. With as_of, an Employment Situation row counts as known 10 days after month end. A settlement period the catalog already holds is an error: query it.

FLAGS. You MUST state every flag returned: seasonal_adjustment_mismatch, last_period_before_settlement (more than one period between the last row and settlement), rounding_unverified, rounding_mismatch, units_mismatch, history_gap, history_stale, series_not_sourced. units_mismatch and history_stale block the scan. Check a Kalshi edge with backtest_market_forecast(source='kalshi', series=<venue series, e.g. KXPAYROLLS>) when confidence.backtest is null.

recipes.title: GDP and recession events on Kalshi or Polymarket: the forecast builder does not resolve them, so build the forecast from the tables and pass it in
recipes.body:
Driver output (title matches gdp or recession; tables econ.gdp_statistics and econ.real_gdp_growth; basis release) has no settlement-series resolver in the forecast builder. price_market_event(build_forecast=true) and forecast_market_event fail with "driver 'output' has no settlement-series resolver in the builder", and scan_market_opportunities lists the event under not_forecast as unresolved. That is the tool's behaviour for this driver, not an absent forecast.

forecast_market_event accepts a series override with frequency monthly, weekly or daily only, so a quarterly series cannot be given to it. Build the forecast by hand:
1) price_market_event(source, event_id) with no forecast: read the rules for the exact release (estimate and vintage), period, units and rounding.
2) describe_table on econ.gdp_statistics and econ.real_gdp_growth, then query the series the rules name. Check data_coverage: how many quarters lie between the table's last period and the settlement period.
3) A release forecast goes in as arima_forecast on that series with forecast and forecast_std_error at the settlement period, passed to price_market_event as mean and sd; or as samples_sql of historical period-over-period changes applied to the latest level (first column the settlement value, one row per sample, no NULLs, under 5000 rows). A regression forecast (ols_regression, flexible_regression) is cross_validate-d first.
4) Pass round when the rules settle to a precision.

Price the event on each venue with the same forecast. A forecast you pass in has no engine backtest: price_market_event reports confidence weak with the reason 'the forecast was given by the caller', and that is to be stated with the edge. A recession event settles on whatever its rules define: read them and forecast that quantity; where no catalog series gives it, say that no tool forecasts it and do not price it against a forecast of another quantity.

recipes.title: Forecasting a mortgage-rate or housing event on Kalshi or Polymarket: weekly 30-year rate, starts, permits, Case-Shiller, and the flags that always appear on a longer horizon
recipes.body:
Drivers mortgage_rate (title matches mortgage rate) and housing (housing starts, home sales, home prices, building permits) are resolved in part. Build with price_market_event(source, event_id, build_forecast=true) or forecast_market_event(source, event_id), for the event on each venue.

MORTGAGE RATE. MORTGAGE30US, the 30-year fixed rate, weekly, percent (econ.fred_indicators). A rate named '15-year' is not resolved (the catalog series is the 30-year): the call fails and asks for series and table. Default transform level, additive: historical h-period changes in percentage points added to the latest rate, h = ceil(days from the last row to the settlement date / 7); the settlement date is the event's close date unless settlement_period (an ISO date) is given. Default history is 10 years of weekly rows.
